Recent developments in Gromov-Wasserstein distance have led to a greater understanding of the topological features in networks. This has significant implications for identifying similar topological structures in various fields, such as biology and physics. However, concerns about data privacy, particularly when dealing with sensitive medical or physical data, necessitate careful consideration. In the face of potential leaks, even if insignificant, secure data protection becomes essential. The challenge of protecting node-wise private data in networks while preserving topological metrics for community detection has emerged as a crucial issue. To address this, we introduce a private-friendly graph discrepancy metric based on Gromov-Wasserstein distance, suitable for distributed node-wise graphs with diverse vertex degrees. This metric has two applications: first, it helps maintain the original topology of aggregated nodes while ensuring differential privacy, and second, it facilitates the analysis of a synthetic dataset generated from a private healthcare network. The proposed metric is demonstrated through simulation on a synthetic healthcare network.

Recent experiments at the high repetition rate COBRA facility have shown that using a laser pulse with its polarization changed en route to the target is an effective method of limiting electron injection through the plasma by an unmodified laser pulse. This experimental result is supported by simulations modeling the interaction between the laser pulse and the plasma, including the transition from Gudmundsson to Q1D model equations. The data from these simulations shows that a change in polarization occurs naturally as the laser pulse passes through the plasma, suggesting that such a method could be used to control electron injection into the plasma by adjusting the laser pulse's polarization.

The study conducted at the Laboratori Nazionali del Gran Sasso using the CRESST experiment's technique for searching for rare events found no evidence to indicate the occurrence of any unusual decay or induction process within a platinum sample. Based on the analysis of 192.5 kg of platinum with a 300-day exposure, at a 90% confidence level, the following limits were established for various events: double beta decay via the capture of an electron, with rates less than $2\cdot10^{17},\, 4\cdot10^{17}$ and $1\cdot10^{19}$ disintegrations per year and kilogram for electron captures by virtue of the exchange of leptons, with rates less than $1\cdot10^{-8}$ and $1\cdot10^{-9}$ events per year and kilogram for dark matter-induced processes via the mediators vine and phion, with rates less than $7\cdot10^{-15}$ and $1\cdot10^{-16}$ events per year and kilogram. Furthermore, the study explored the possibility of detecting dark matter particles at masses ranging from several thousand to ten thousand Thomson masses, with rates less than $1\cdot10^{-42}$ and $1\cdot10^{-43} events per year and kilogram.

The value of the dimensional regularization parameter is used to calculate the mass-dependent components of QCD's anomaly and the corresponding charge renormalization, specifically within the $\overline{\text{MS}}$ scheme. A detailed derivation is provided in the context of massless TW scheme, leading to the conclusion that a unique value of $\epsilon$ is required for the anomaly calculation. The simplicity of the anomaly equation is preserved even after introducing the mass-dependent charge renormalization through the $\overline{\text{MS}}$ scheme conversion, where a consistent value of $\epsilon$ is applied equally to both the anomalous and renormalization parts. A contrast is drawn with the $\overline{\text{MS}}$ scheme calculation that initiates the calculation with a general $\epsilon$ before simplifying at the end of the calculation, which is akin to a specific limit of $\epsilon$.

The absence of semantic camera calibration in standard 3D reconstruction and object segmentation leads to inaccurate predictions on real-world data with different camera orientations. Our proposed method, cross-camera deep tinting, overcomes this limitation and allows object predictions to be consistent across various camera perspectives by fusing predictions from multiple cameras. This approach adapts an existing object segmentation network by introducing a module that aligns object features across cameras. The modular network design maintains the efficiency and performance of the original base model, enabling easy integration into existing object segmentation systems. The proposed method demonstrates improved performance on several benchmark tests, including PASCAL, CUB, and CARS, particularly when handling out-of-distribution data with different camera perspectives.

This study reveals the underlying symmetries of a modified, n-dimensional model proposed by Levi-Civita and Fokas. We derive the corresponding consistency conditions for potential symmetries within this model. We also investigate the preservation of these symmetries in the context of a specific class of conservative integrable systems of dimension n. Furthermore, our analysis demonstrates the connection between the Levi-Civita-Fokas model and the Ermakov system.

Building a Transit Feed Specification (TFS) allows a platform to integrate and provide real-time transportation data to users, with standardization being key to this process. Current platforms relying on this standard face a key challenge: many transportation providers lack the resources to create this required data standard by contributing a TFS. To address this issue, we propose using Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) to estimate a missing TFS based on historical data collected from Feed Binary Format (FBF), which is an open protocol for sharing and processing transportation feed. In our research, we collected and combined multiple feeds and created synthetic datasets to compare different RNN models. Ultimately, we adapted a variant of the LSTM model and developed UNO-TFS-NN, an RNN model that accurately predicts and generates a TFS for unknown transportation providers. Through experiments using real-world datasets, UNO-TFS-NN demonstrated the ability to successfully create a feasible and accurate TFS for various scenarios such as route and schedule changes.

In few-shot classification, having representative knowledge of categories can significantly aid. Traditional approaches typically define prototypes as the mean features of the classes' training examples. However, this method has its drawbacks, as it fails to capture that certain categories may have more training data, thereby compromising its ability to accurately represent those classes. To address this limitation, we suggest developing "prototypes" that represent categories at a higher level, specifically using meta-learning. By doing so, we can leverage these prototypes to classify novel shots and improve classification outcomes, even when the classes' training and novel shot data diverge significantly. When compared to the standard prototype approach, our scheme excels, especially in scenarios with disparate training and novel data.

We're analyzing systems that have an edge in a 2+1 dimensional spacetime environment, classified by continuous symmetry properties. Our findings reveal that a specific subset of these systems, characterized by non-invertible symmetry groups, can exhibit distinct features where the symmetry remains unchanged even after the system's boundary conditions are compactified. Consequently, a standard theorem applying to such cases predicts that these systems, having no net edge or being fully surrounded, will inevitably lack a one-to-one mapping. Furthermore, we propose a new equation that accurately describes the relationship between the symmetry properties and the system's edge characteristics in these non-invertible cases. Our research provides evidence and supporting examples to validate these conclusions within the frameworks of conformal field theory and quantum Chern-Simons theory.

A semi-transitive triangle in a directed graph, like the one formed by Edmonds, is defined as a triangle where the edge from one vertex to the middle vertex does not connect to the edge from the middle vertex to the third vertex. Split graphs are graphs that can be broken down into a bipartite graph and a clique. For split graphs, researchers explored semi-transitivity. They proved that identifying semi-transitivity in split graphs of degree two is an NP-complete problem and finds it within polynomial time when the problem is non-cooperative. Additionally, when the problem is cooperative, researchers found an exponential time algorithm but showed no NP-completeness. In further study, researchers identified when semi-transitivity is guaranteed in specific types of split graphs, such as bipartite graphs and a particular type of split graph called P_5-free split graphs.

A cutting-edge approach has been developed to accurately identify genuine hadronic tau decays in the CMS detector, distinguishing them from those originating from quarks, gluons, electrons, and muons. By incorporating insights from neighboring particles, this novel method utilizes a sophisticated deep neural network to analyze complex data. As a result, it exhibits marked performance improvements over its predecessor, particularly in effectively differentiating between tau decays and those involving quarks, at a rate of 25 to 30 percent. Moreover, it achieves an exceptionally high level of accuracy in correctly categorizing tau decays, such as those from electrons or muons, at rates exceeding 95 percent. This advanced approach will serve as a foundation for future hadronic tau decay studies in the CMS detector.

Future deep sky observations are expected to yield vast amounts of data, 
generating an inflection point where data analysis becomes too intricate for humans alone 
to process, even with the assistance of a computer. To rectify this issue, employ probabilistic approaches 
that can consolidate knowledge acquired from various learning strategies. Based on the concept of Bayesian networks, 
we develop a system comprising Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs) capable of seamlessly integrating multiple training sets 
and calculating uncertainty levels for each prediction. To utilize these BNNs effectively, we incorporate them into 
a decision tree framework, dubbed IRT, which incorporates inference and predicts uncertainty levels. We utilize this 
framework to categorize objects in the Milky Way, specifically supernova remnants (SRs) and pulsars (PSRs), utilizing 
the SR catalog generated by the Deep Learning based SR classifier (DL_SR) and the PSR catalog created by the Neural Network 
Pulsar classification (NN_PS), and examining the results for both models to determine their accuracy and reliability 
for subsequent thorough investigations. We compare the results of IRT with those of the human classifier S2, who correctly identified $80\%$ of SRs and $100\%$ of PSRs, whereas IRT accurately categorized $80\%$ of SRs and $90\%$ of PSRs. Furthermore, our model successfully predicted an absolute magnitude value within a $0.5$ magnitude margin of error for both catalogs. Through

Our study delves into the phenomenon of forward Brillouin scattering across modal interactions within solid-core photonic lattice fibers, complemented by statistical modeling and experimental validation. By operating the fiber Brillouin gain band through adjustment of the pump frequency, we identify an optimal setting for efficient mechanical mode coupling. Furthermore, we observe the absence of spatial mode coupling in hollow-core fibers and attribute this to random azimuthal deposition of nanocrystalline sulfur ink.

The Coxeter group foundation theorem, primarily studied in solvable groups, states that any minimal generating set of a solvable Coxeter group naturally divides into two sets: one consisting of arbitrary elements and another consisting of highly reducible elements with a base generating set having a specific degree of reducibility. We expand on this theorem by establishing a new result for B-type Coxeter groups, defining a generating set as foundational if it consists of two parts: one set of elements that can generate a spherical subgroup and another set of elements that together generate a subgroup isomorphic to $A_{k-1}$. We establish a foundational generating set characterization for simple B-type Coxeter groups and partially generalize the result to more complex B-type groups.

The continuous optimization of resource allocation under constraints has been a long-standing challenge in operations research and computer science. A particular issue is the cost-benefit analysis of items with varying costs and benefits, where the optimal strategy involves selecting a subset of items to maximize overall benefit while staying within budget. This problem has two variants, known as the Set-Union Knapsack Problem (SUKP) and the Budgeted Maximum Coverage Problem (BMCP), which differ in their approach to covering targets with selected items. Both variants are highly parallelizable and can be efficiently solved on modern computing architectures, making them ideal candidates for high-performance computing. We propose a novel, versatile local search solution for SUKP and BMCP, which rapidly (near) globally optimal solutions with superior speed and efficiency compared to existing parallel solutions. A comprehensive evaluation of our method involves analyzing its performance on a large dataset of problem instances and comparing it to the current state-of-the-art cross-entropy method.

Churn rate reduction in the online gaming sector is a key priority for gaming operators. By applying advanced segmentation and predictive modeling techniques, informed decision-making can be achieved which minimize churn and maximize long-term customer retention. A crucial step in achieving this goal is developing robust churn probability models for individual players, allowing operators to identify those most likely to leave and allocate resources effectively to retain them. Despite the widespread use of machine learning in sports betting loss prediction, there is a lack of available models for predicting player churn, making this a missing link in the industry. Therefore, this project aims to develop and test machine learning models for predicting player churn, utilizing data from a real-world online gaming environment. A comprehensive approach is employed, starting with data preparation and categorization through target variable labeling and feature engineering, before building and fine-tuning the primary model. By using advanced machine learning and statistical methods, two primary models are created: probability and rank models, which are then validated to ensure their effectiveness. Further analysis of the models reveals insights into the variables that drive player churn, allowing operators to develop tailored retention strategies tailored to the specific needs of different customers. Surprisingly, despite the prominence of rewards as a key player churn risk factor, only a limited number of customers in the dataset were identified as being at risk of churn due to rewards issues. This highlights opportunities for gaming operators to identify and address reward-related risks earlier.

We examine the two-dimensional Ising model under a uniform magnetic field using high-temperature series expansions up to the 10th order. We determine the specific heat and magnetization expansions around the Yang-Lee critical point, yielding exact expansion results for the first 10 terms and plausible estimates for higher order terms. We find that the expansion correctly places all critical points, including the Yang-Lee singular point, and accurately represents the critical exponents. We represent the specific heat and magnetization through a sum of logarithmic terms and their corresponding critical dimensionless ratios, placing these ratios on an isospectral axis, equating them to corresponding critical points of the pure Ising model. We interpret the results by applying the analytical properties of the Ising model's bare correlation functions and transferring this information to the physical renormalization group. We also derive a comprehensive list of dimensionless ratios based on high-temperature expansions up to the 10th order.

The LMT PDFs and TMDs for gluons have been unknown due to theoretical obstacles. Recent research utilizing the LMT approach has provided an analytical framework for extracting gluon TMDs from LHC data on dijet distributions. With this new understanding, it becomes apparent that non-perturbative effects play a significant role in the evolution of gluon TMDs between the probe and target. By incorporating these factors along with in-in resummation and parton parton scattering processes, it has been possible to derive a practical calculable distribution for gluon TMDs. This innovative approach now makes it feasible to extract the gluon TMDs from experimental data, thereby promoting a new understanding of the gluon and its role in hadronic collisions.

In the photon-photon interaction that occurs during ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions, electron-positron pairs are produced through a process called photon-photon fusion, resulting in a broad range of lepton creation in space around the collision point. Those electron-positron pairs formed near dense nuclei experience additional interactions, such as electron-positron pair annihilation or electromagnetic radiation, until they are detected at a collider experiment's sensor locations. This work focuses on the detailed electromagnetic interactions involving charged leptons produced through photon-photon fusion in the early stages of collisions. Calculations are provided for electron-positron pair annihilation, direct emission, and bremsstrahlung loss in the presence of dense nuclei, including transport factors in the context of relativistic nuclei colliding at varying energies. This research also considers identified lepton production in interactions involving a single nucleus or multiple nuclei at varying lengths of interaction with photons, including transport factors in the context of relativistic nuclei at varying energies. This is applied to examples of electron-positron pair annihilation, direct emission, and bremsstrahlung loss in the presence of dense nuclei at collider experiment data collections.

To minimize pollution, bicycle usage is experiencing a resurgence, especially in urban environments. Despite the trend towards decreased fatalities in other traffic groups, the opposite holds true for cyclists. Therefore, tracking cyclist data is essential to improving their safety by providing city planners with data to design safer cycling routes. This study proposes a comprehensive approach to developing cyclist safety maps by leveraging video-based automatic incident detection. The proposed method involves training a multi-task cognitive network to simulate human risk assessment when navigating a scenario. This network incorporates a context-aware risk descriptor inspired by human perception, allowing it to consider factors such as speed, route elevation, and the presence of potentially hazardous elements. The results show that the proposed descriptor can effectively identify and analyze cyclist incidents. Additionally, the study highlights the benefits and drawbacks of utilizing different cognitive network structures. While the proposed method holds promise, it has several limitations, including a limited dataset and a reliance on high-performance computational hardware.

This research proposes a novel framework that enables robots to safely navigate complex and unpredictable environments through the integration of adaptive control barrier functions, random fuzzy modeling, and Tikhonov regularization. By incorporating the key characteristics of human behavior and movement constraints into a unified model, this framework effectively captures both the dynamics of human trajectories and the moral obligations of robot actions. To navigate environments where other agents may intervene, this framework incorporates a predictive model that accounts for the actions and intentions of these agents. Simulations of a robot moving through a space influenced by a group of potential obstacles demonstrate the proposed method's ability to develop and implement safety protocols proactively, even in scenarios where the obstacles' actions are unknown or motivated by malicious motives.

For a ring R, its enveloping numbers N(R) are defined as the set where each element satisfies two conditions: it square is within the ring and its square root is also within the ring. The study of (square root) enveloping numbers in various types of rings has significant implications. Research has shown that these numbers have numerous applications in determining prime graphs, p-autocompleteness, fundamental rings, and ideal properties. As a result, identifying methods to create rings with enveloping numbers is a high priority. This research aims to establish a method for constructing rings with enveloping numbers and demonstrate its usefulness in understanding nil rings, prime rings, square-zero rings, Boolean rings, and perfect rings.

As deep neural networks become more involved in high-stakes missions, the likelihood increases that they will encounter malicious or subversive input data intended to disrupt their operation or extract sensitive information. While research has largely focused on neural network development for various applications, the study of adversarial resilience is critical for ensuring the reliable operation of these networks in real-world scenarios. This work aims to enhance the robustness of neural networks by investigating a novel approach that leverages natural language to protect against adversarial attacks. Specifically, a dual-module framework is proposed that incorporates an adversarial detection module to identify potentially malicious input data and a mitigation module to prevent or minimize the impact of such attacks by modifying the input parameters. This approach was tested using two datasets, which revealed its effectiveness in detecting adversarial attacks for language-based applications and significantly reduce their impact on task accuracy, while utilizing a relatively simple adversarial detection model.

The nonlocal conservation laws with flux functions of the form $f(u(x,t))$, where $u$ is a function of two variables, space and time, are studied in conservation law theory. Under the condition that the function $f$ is convex, along with additional constraints, it is proven that solutions to these laws are unique, stable, and subject to specific constraints regarding their behavior and any initial disturbances that may occur. The proof relies on an innovative method where solutions are reinterpreted as a type of nonlocal fluid flow problem, and entropy admissibility is directly linked to the properties of the function $f$. It is found that for convex functions there is only one possible admissible shock for a broad class of conserved quantities, and a detailed calculation of the rate at which solutions converge to their limiting form is provided, with results that generalize prior work and provide new insights for mathematicians working in this field.

A dilation surface is an embedded surface in 4-dimensional space that has a specific scaling factor greater than or equal to one, applied from within. Considering infinite dilation surfaces, we identify two distinct types, finite dilation surfaces that conform to a specific structure called a saddle link and those that exhibit a specific repeating pattern geometrically. Our findings show that a dilation surface with the saddle link structure has a specific characteristic, implementing a new concept called a horizon saddle link, and using this, we demonstrate a specific classification system for dilation surfaces based on their dynamics. Additionally, we identify specific boundary surfaces associated with infinite dilation surfaces and finite dilation surfaces respectively, and show that they both belong to a specific class of surfaces that maintain a consistent pattern under a specific type of contraction, known as retraction surfaces.

Recent studies have suggested using total correlation to measure functional connectivity between brain regions to inform theories of cognitive abilities and behavioral data. In this study, we used resting-state fMRI data from the 1000 Subjects Functional Connectome Project to examine relationships between regional brain activity. Specifically, we found substantial evidence supporting the importance of local and nearby regions, while further analysis revealed relatively weak correlations between more distant brain areas. These results are consistent with the concept of brain regions communicating in intricate networks. Moreover, we observed consistent evidence of higher connectivity within and among adjacent brain networks, which was similar across all subjects. In line with these findings, our analysis of cross-subject correlations yielded similar total correlation patterns. Finally, we discovered similarities between regional brain connectivity and the structural connections shared by brain regions, which was confirmed through an examination of correlations at both the group and individual levels. These findings provide fresh insights into brain communication and encourage the development of new theories and models.

This work introduces an in-depth exploration of the Segal-Bargmann transformation in the context of Clifford algebra, examining its underlying mathematical structure and its association with the Taylor isomorphism between the spaces of Hermitian and continuous functions on a real Clifford algebra. The investigation relies on the principles of analytic continuation and functional differentiation to establish a comprehensive understanding of the Clifford algebra-based Segal-Bargmann transformation and verify its connection to the Taylor isomorphism. The study, presented in two parts (one focusing on the SB transformation's representation, the other on its connection to the isomorphism), relies on a consistent method of calculation based on the bosonic structure of the Clifford algebra. The calculation involves both left- and right-action strategies in the context of the algebra. Additionally, two supporting appendices have been included to provide further explanation and context. The first examines the relationship between the Clifford group and its associated coordinate system, while the second presents a concise overview of the Hermitian function space in a real Clifford algebra framework.

For a Gaussian field with stationary, continuous, ergodic, and analytic properties, we define the notion of path-wise conditioning based on a set of real-valued, continuous, and stationary functions. Our work builds upon this construction and explores its various applications across statistical physics, statistical mechanics, and partial differential equations, particularly for identifying minimizing object's characteristics in energy functions and finding solutions to partial differential equations that are dependent on unknown variables within those equations. To facilitate this, we employ a technique that involves linearization and the use of conditioning to establish a characterizing equation for such objects, similar to how the method of variations of constants is applied in the context of differential equations.

This research explores the feasibility of creating a hybrid ground-and-air sensor network that generates real-time, multi-spatial-frequency data collection. A ground-based autonomous utility vehicle, equipped with a 3D multi-beam antenna, tracks aerial vehicles that carry sensors gathering environmental and structural data. We demonstrate the accuracy of real-time, high-resolution mapping in diverse environments using inertial navigation and multi-beam antenna technologies. Our approach involves integrating satellite data with multi-beam antenna positioning to achieve accurate vehicle navigation. The successful integration of this system in various testing environments, including coastal scans and structural inspections, validates its potential for wide-range applications, potentially including search-and-rescue operations, environmental monitoring, and infrastructure assessments.

We are on the cusp of a breakthrough in long-range neutrino research due to a forthcoming series of large-scale experiments, incorporating both land-based and underwater/ice-based detectors. The latter have the added benefit of being well-suited to address mysteries related to core-collapse supernovae, proton decay, and Neutrino Oscillations over long distances, albeit at the expense of greater technical complexity. Specifically, we will examine the roles of the JUNO and DUNE experiments in dissecting neutrino physics, with a focus on DUNE's curation of the most extreme, long-distance neutrino observations. Both JUNO and DUNE are designed to offer precision measurements of various neutrino phenomena, with DUNE maintaining a unique position to investigate the neutrino-argon cross-section and related matters of fundamental importance.

A crucial element in the search for top partners is an efficient top tagging algorithm. This study presents an improved top tagging algorithm with enhanced signal rejection and improved background rejection capabilities. Compared to the standard top tagging algorithm, it demonstrates superior performance, reducing the amount of background events by 20% to 30% without increasing the confusion with signal events. The authors have also employed a novel strategy to validate the effectiveness of this algorithm and other similar top tagging methods, using a technique inspired by the Cockcroft-Wilson method. This new approach, which is based on experimentally measured quantities, provides a more robust and reliable method for top tagging validation. However, this method is only applicable in scenarios where the top partner decay mode is large compared to other modes.

This document establishes a foundation for accurately representing Virtual Organizations within distributed systems, encompassing their practical implementation and the consequences on system operation, as well as the underlying conceptual definition of VO characteristics. A general model of VO properties has been developed and is presented in this report. Additionally, we have formally defined a particular Virtual Organization, known as Stochastic VO (SVo), which possesses distinct properties enabling straightforward analysis. The report also outlines a method for transitioning from standard VO characteristics to SVo characteristics, effectively transforming any VO into an analyzable form.

To effectively accelerate reinforcement learning (RL) training, experience replay has become a crucial component in many algorithms, particularly those utilizing off-policy methods. However, the current approaches that incorporate sampling from a replay buffer are detrimental to TD-based optimization methods, as they result in a random distribution of data that hampers the capture of temporal dependencies in time-series data. Building upon previous research, we introduce an improved approach called VarDE, which modifies the replay buffer to prioritize samples that closely reflect the agent's optimal policy, thereby accelerating the learning process. By prioritizing samples that match the agent's optimal policy, VarDE effectively enhances temporal dependencies and accelerates the agent's learning process. Furthermore, VarDE's adjusted replay buffer is compatible with a wide range of TD-based optimization methods, as it simply modifies the sampling distribution from which the agent selects data. We validate VarDE's efficacy on multiple challenging robotics scenarios, demonstrating its potential for improved performance.

Two new transformations, the superbosonization and the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation, have been proposed to tackle integrals of odd powers of bosons. Although they share a common goal, these transformations differ in their approach, with the superbosonization relying on bosonization in the coordinate space and the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation using the momentum space. We delve into the relationship between these two transformations, applying them to a specific problem: the $k$-dependent Gaussian integral in the momentum space. By applying both transformations to this problem, we derive the same result, thus establishing a direct correlation between these two approaches. Furthermore, we apply the superbosonization method to a more complex problem: the integral of odd powers of bosons in the coordinate space, which leads to the derivation of the variances and covariances of field operators in the presence of a chemical potential.

A promising approach called motion forecasting utilizes kinematic data for predicting future object movements. Nevertheless, the current formulation of motion forecasting as predicting future object positions overlooks the inherent aspects of motion such as direction, velocity, and acceleration. Moreover, object position data can be misleading and prone to errors during the forecasting process, for instance when multiple objects are positioned at the same location. To resolve these issues, we introduce a novel method called MoDeRNN, which uses a novel RNN component to represent motion aspects like velocity and acceleration. We show that representing motion in this way with residual errors provides more accuracy and interpretability of the forecasting results. Additionally, we examine how representing motion aspects impacts the performance of motion forecasting and other related tasks like optical flow estimation and action recognition. Experimental results on two challenging real-world datasets, for motion forecasting and action recognition, demonstrate that MoDeRNN outperforms other methods used in motion forecasting.

This research focuses on blending Rust and JavaScript within a unified online framework. We've leveraged advanced web capabilities to create a real-time, client-side memory model, which facilitates secure data exchange between languages. Our innovative approach encodes Rust's memory management rules, making it feasible to represent Rust objects as usable and safe entities within JavaScript, and vice versa. Additionally, we've developed novel anti-patterns that necessitate manual polynomial-time processing, and a novel anti-pattern pattern illustrating the challenges of frequent, rapid data transformations involving Rust and JavaScript.

Studies have discovered new forms of neutrinoless double-beta decay that involve
a combination of neutrino flavors and multiple exponents in the coupling constants.
We investigate the interplay between these exotic decay processes using the
intermediate-scale left-right models as a reference point. In particular, we've
created tables illustrating how variations in collider energies affect the
ratio between different types of decay events, which could be crucial in identifying
these novel phenomena at future collider experiments.

Yet, to further minimize these costs, it is necessary to utilize the subcode in a more efficient manner possible. This is achieved through the utilization of a subcode based parity-check matrix that gets added to the original parity-check matrix of the polar code. The process of combining multiple images involves altering their relative scale and position, which in turn triggers questions about the nature of the point spread functions of the resulting combined images. This research addresses those questions by developing a mathematical framework for deriving the point spread functions of combined images. To achieve this, we introduce a novel concept called a scale-invariant convolution, which is a linear image transformation operator. By defining this operator for a variable scaling factor, we demonstrate its application in combining images of arbitrary sizes. Next, we establish a mathematical relationship between the point spread functions of the original images and that of their combined counterpart. As a result, we demonstrate the ability to calculate the point spread function of combined images without explicit knowledge of their original pixel arrangements. As a demonstration of its practical utility, we examine a specific scenario where the scale factor is uniform across a region of interest. In addition, we discuss an application of our developed technique, which involves utilizing a shift-invariant diffraction model to correct for optical wavefront distortions in image capture devices.

The fracture strength of solid crystals is examined, focusing on the primary and secondary influences. Primary factors determine the fracture strength by creating or impeding crack growth. Implications of these fracture mechanisms are derived for material design, testing, and analysis. Secondary factors can either favorably alter fracture strengths or introduce undesirable effects, though their impact is generally contained due to the predominantly favorable crack growth triggered by the primary factors.

We examine the relationship between the half-plane Gaussian free field and multiple SLEs driven by a complex-valued Gaussian process. The field and the processes share a common connection to a complex-valued bulk critical fermionic operator in a two-dimensional conformal field theory. Specifically, we study the statistics of the field's real part within the half-plane by relating it to the real part of the driving function of the multiple SLEs beyond the upper half-plane. This enables us to obtain the field's correlation kernel by conditioning a determinantal point process associated with the multiple SLEs to have zero imaginary components. The resulting kernel exhibits alternating point process properties known as "inverted" and "standard" depending on the test point's location relative to the underlying external source. By invoking the PDE characterization of the field, we establish that the multiple SLEs' statistics, specifically the y-evolution of the process, is equivalent to the field's point source correlation. Ultimately, we align these findings with the prior work on Gaussian free fields coupled with SLEs driven by a single complex-valued Gaussian process.

In this research, we address the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations in multi-dimensional space with smooth periodic initial conditions and obtain analytical estimates based on a function's maximum value. These estimates are relevant to the 2D case and can also be applied to 3 or more dimensions.

The verification task for a quantum computation involves ensuring that a quantum circuit produces a desired output.  We have developed a traditional verification method that runs in linear time and can verify quantum computations for any number of qubits, regardless of their complexity.  Our approach uses a balance matrix to represent the quantum circuit's action on its qubits, allowing us to translate the verification task into a balance problem.  By representing states as linear combinations of bases, known as Koopman vectors, we can adapt angular autocorrelation matrices to traditional verification.  Furthermore, we have shown that our method can be used in conjunction with quantum annealers, like the D-Wave system, to speed up the optimization process of complex binary problems.  We have successfully applied our traditional verification method to various problems, such as the Max 2-SAT problem, and observed a significant reduction in running time compared to classical solvers like the Trun D-Wave and classical D-Wave's classical equivalent.

A blockchain system enables secure interaction among parties with conflicting reliability, by guaranteeing the immutability and reachability of distributed data. The integration of blockchain technology with Internet of Things (IoT) systems, known as Industrial Blockchain, is a promising application of this system. The process of developing an industrial blockchain is complex and requires specific guidelines to ensure the correct assessment and integration of IoT sources. The selection of an appropriate blockchain architecture is a critical step in designing an industrial blockchain application. The process of selecting a blockchain configuration is difficult and requires significant resources. The lack of standardized frameworks and guidelines to support industrial blockchain development is a significant obstacle to success. We present a new framework for developing industrial blockchain applications, featuring a modular architecture that consists of following key components: IoT sources, smart contracts, blockchain platforms, oracles, and management software. The framework specifies a ten-step process for developing industrial blockchain applications. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework by presenting a real-world use case that involves the food supply chain, showing how our framework can be used to develop a secure and transparent food supply chain blockchain application.

Artificial intelligence has successfully modeled grains, animals, and plants to perfect proportions; however, replicating living cells proves particularly challenging. Since these cells vary greatly and are subject to external influences, creating a universal representation of their shape is the initial hurdle in developing an effective generative model. Our approach involves training a representation of cell walls separate from their labels, using a universal representation called an implicit function, which can accurately describe complex three-dimensional shapes from a compact encoding. By applying this function globally or localizing it to specific regions, we can successfully generate full cell walls from compactly stored information. Our representations of cell walls can also successfully classify cell types and predict the progress of cellular diseases. Notably, our method benefits from recent advancements in universal function approximation, allowing us to generate a vast variety of synthetic cell types after only a short training time.

The concept of navigability in documents has been understudied, particularly in relation to the challenges faced by print-disabled individuals. To address this gap, our research delves into making documents accessible to visually impaired and other print-disabled group members. In this research, we identified essential requirements for making documents understandable by investigating the strategies used by sighted individuals when interacting with printed documents. These participants were asked to follow a defined sequence when examining a set of documents that included introductions, summaries, tables, articles, and drafts. Through an examination of their thought processes and subsequent questioning, we established six key conditions necessary for making documents navigable. These conditions can be applied across various formats, including braille, audio, and digital versions of documents. Furthermore, our research highlights the significance of understanding document navigability in enhancing existing methods of making documents accessible to the print impaired.

While BERT excels at modeling bidirectional contexts through denoising autoencoding, its reliance on input masking overlooks positional dependencies, leading to inconsistent pretraining-finetune performance. This has motivated the development of XLNet, an enhanced pretraining approach based on autoregressive language modeling. This method enables bidirectional contextual learning through the integration of permutations of factorization order and, consequently, enforces a comprehensive set of data-level pretraining objectives. Notably, XLNet achieves superior performance on 20 benchmarks, including improvements on 15 GRACE challenges. Moreover, empirical analysis indicates that the achieved success stems from its capability in harmoniously balancing bidirectional contextual learning and positional autoregressive modeling.

We've developed computational models aimed at assessing the impact of stellar activity on spectroscopic analysis of exoplanet transits, particularly focusing on atmospheric characterization, in systems with both low and high resolution spectroscopic data. We've analyzed the effects of stellar activity on different atmospheric models, discovering that activity levels equivalent to 100 ppm can distort atmospheric composition clues by at least the same amount, a concern that will persist until advanced mitigation techniques are developed. To mitigate these effects in low-resolution spectroscopy, we've investigated the effectiveness of subtracting mean stellar spectra, a popular approach. Although successful in most cases with minimal spectral overlap, we've found this method falls short when there are multiple planets, as well as in certain atmospheric scenarios. Ultimately, we conclude that achieving precision better than the level required to identify the dominant atmospheric components will necessitate advanced mitigation techniques or accurate stellar activity maps, both of which are challenging to achieve, particularly for distant or low-resolution target stars. High-resolution spectroscopy, on the other hand, offers a more effective means of extracting this information, but this comes with its own set of limitations, such as constraints on the energy range as determined by the target star's properties and available observational time.

We are given a Riemann surface, denoted as $S$, equipped with a metric called $g_0$, which has the following properties: it is a complex analytic metric, consistent with a given conformal structure and with a finite number of cone points. If $G$ represents the set of all such metrics meeting these conditions and if $c$ signifies half the minimum integer value of the cone angles at the exceptional points, then the family of metrics, $\mathcal{F}_{g_0,c}$, consisting of all elements that coincide with $g_0$ near the exceptional points and have a curvature bounded by $b>0$, is dense in the metric space for any given $c\leq0$ and for any $g_0\in G$. This theoretical framework is relevant to the study of generalized hyperbolicity in surfaces with changing shapes.

Research into the swimming motion of the centipede forficatus near the surface of water-water interface shows it doesn't use its 14 leg pairs primarily for movement; instead of most aquatic animals that move by alternating movements of their legs, this species moves more efficiently by utilizing 3-5 leg pairs at a time. These extra leg pairs are thought to mainly play a supporting role in reducing vibrations in the force generated while the creature moves. Using high-speed cameras and advanced simulations, our study shows that secondary leg pairs contribute up to 20% of the total movement force but only account for 30% of the movement speed, supporting previous findings on such quadrupeds as the frog and the human, our research further suggests that using extra limb support during movement is called for by the fluid dynamics of the movement of the lightweight forficatus.

A novel from 2013, "The Three-Body Problem" by Liu Cixin, depicts a devastating asteroid impact that causes widespread destruction through a tsunami, but this scenario has not been thoroughly studied scientifically. Our goal in this research project is to examine the dispersal of the tsunami resulting from a massive impact on Earth's equatorial region through linear flux splitting technique within the Euler-Lagrange framework. This study involves presenting the results of a high-resolution model over 600 degrees of longitude and 100 meters water depth resolution, which would require substantial computational resources. To achieve this, we first present the dispersal dynamics of the tsunami waves generated by the impact in the southern Pacific Ocean through a coarse 4-kilometer resolution model. We then introduce an adaptive, 100-meter resolution model that focuses on critical regions and seamlessly interfaces with the coarse-resolution model at specified interfaces. Both models utilize 11 components based on the moment-of-magnitude theory to adapt to varying computational costs and display impressive convergence at respective levels of resolution. Ultimately, we envision integrating these models into a fully coupled, ecosystem-ocean-atmosphere system to simulate the asteroid impact's effects in real-time scenarios.

Using newly available James Webb Space Telescope data, researchers have identified a new class of galaxies - high-star-forming, massive galaxies that were missed by past observations because of their low brightness in the optical range. These galaxies, which appear bright in the infrared spectrum, started producing stars intensely, possibly due to the way they are viewed, not a change in their actual star formation rates. Based on the information gathered, scientists determined the nature of these galaxies using a new method, which combines the analysis of their infrared emission with the possible effects of distant objects and dust in the line of sight. These galaxies, which appear bright in the infrared spectrum, are found to be large, massive and highly star-forming, with the majority consisting of late-type galaxies, which show a higher rate of star formation, are smaller in size and have different structural properties compared to their early-type galaxy counterparts. These newly found data, which are providing a better and broader view of galaxy evolution, are challenging our current understanding and it has been proposed that these galaxies, which appear bright in the infrared spectrum, could have played a major role in the overall rate of star formation across the universe. These findings, which are challenging our current understanding, are opening new avenues of research to gain a better and more complete understanding of galaxy evolution.

This research extends previous work on seven-dimensional Einstein's theory, incorporating geometrical terms into the theory to study their impact. We begin by reviewing the eleven-dimensional supergravity theory, distilling the relevant information from five additional dimensions to establish a seven-dimensional framework for analysis. An eleven-dimensional black hole solution is examined, specifically its simplified form in seven and eleven dimensions, to establish a starting point for investigation. Subsequently, we explore the impact on gravitational potential when two geometrical terms, $\frac{1}{2}\frac{(n-2)(n-3)}{2}\mathcal{R}^2$ and $+\frac{1}{2} R \cdot C_{(0)}$, are introduced into the theory. It is found that these terms alter the gravitational potential such that the potential becomes multipole-dependent and governed by an equation involving radial distance and angular coefficients. Moreover, we derive an equation governing the extent of horizonthal areas in situations where the potential's influence dominates. Finally, we investigate some illustrative examples of black holes displaying this behavior.

Consider a straight channel of length L with rivers flowing through it. The rivers have alternating widths: 2k+1 and 2k+2 units in length. These rivers also have obstructions in the form of horizontal or vertical segments, referred to as "lenses", which cut across the rivers at various widths. The rivers end when they reach the channel's boundaries or encounter overlapping lenses. We're tasked with finding a sequence of lenses to place in the channel so that the difference in length between the two types of rivers is as consistent as possible. This leads to a further optimization problem where we seek to maximize a weighted expression. Our solution involves analyzing alternating sequences of the two rivers, expressed as vectors. We use a graph-based approach to understand how these rivers can intersect and diverge, and apply a tree-like structure to explore all possible scenarios. This exploration enables us to identify when two vertices in the graph are at a finite distance from one another. We also develop algorithms to efficiently compute a scoring function and identify the maximum-scored vertex in the graph. This maximally-scoring vertex corresponds to a sequence of lens lengths that achieves the optimal difference in river lengths. By incorporating weight units to each lens, rather than just their length, we are able to select between different-sized lenses to place in the channel. We're able to prove that under these weighted constraints, the maximum-scored vertex can be efficiently computed through a recursive formula. Two extreme flavors of El Ni\~no have been extensively identified: the central Pacific type (characterized by weaking Easterly Trade Winds and reduced barometric pressure) and the composite pattern of the American Violin. A notable aspect of these flavors is their distinctive impacts on precipitation in the eastern Pacific, Africa, and Indonesia. This research examined the relationship between these flavors and low and excessive seasonal rainfall across the globe. It revealed that the central Pacific El Ni\~no is linked to diminished precipitation in eastern Pacific, Africa, and Indonesia, but in no way guarantees a lack of rainfall in other areas, as suggested by some studies. Additionally, the study found that the central Pacific and the composite pattern of the Violin are not significantly different from the average El Ni\~no in terms of their effects on global rainfall patterns. However, both have distinct impacts on precipitation in the Amazon, with the Violin flavor tending to enhance rainfall while reducing it in the Amazon's western parts, and the central Pacific type decreasing it throughout the region. Further investigation is recommended to determine the underlying causes of the Violin's pattern and its growing prominence during the ongoing climate change.

To examine the development of non-affine, unsymmetrical polymer networks, we created model systems comprising linear and branched molecules that lacked regular structural patterns. As these model systems underwent solvent displacement by non-polar molecules, it was observed that the rate of this displacement could be influenced by both the degree of branch points and the size of the molecules, despite no effect from the initial structural conditions or spatial arrangements. Moreover, it can be inferred that the unsaturated portions of these molecules played a crucial role in the rapid growth of these polymer networks at early stages due to increased interaction with pendant bonds. As a result, these polymer networks exhibited rapid growth near their initial points of dispersion and displayed unusual patterns of scattering. This characteristic unpaid behavior was found to significantly reduce the need for additional monomers in achieving a satisfactory network density. Nonetheless, this rapid growth was eventually hindered by limitations in the availability of unsaturated bonds and the increasing coil dimensions, causing the rate of growth to gradually slow down. This study provides critical insight into the rapid initial growth of complex polymer networks.

The impacts of pollution on populations are significant, and population models provide crucial insights into these effects, particularly for vulnerable species like the populus bubulus, which is at risk due to environmental pollution. To better understand and predict population changes, we developed a mathematical model incorporating age considerations and behavioral influences in a polluted environment. This model is represented by a non-linear differential equation with positive solutions, and we have conducted an analytical examination of its local and global stability using the next-generation matrix and the invariant plane, and it shows that a pollutant such as heavy metal lead can have a detrimental effect on populus bubulus populations. This study aims to provide critical mathematical insights into the impacts of pollution on populations, and the findings suggest that heavy metal lead accumulation can lead to population decline, and possibly extinction. This model can serve as a starting point for more comprehensive population studies incorporating behavioral influences, and offers a framework for predicting population changes and offering practical recommendations to mitigate the effects of pollution on Populus bubulus populations.

The research outcome of this study is the entire spectrum of complexity and decidability findings for a category of very comprehensive logical systems known as hypersequent logics incorporating weakening, contraction, and mixed rules of premisses. Specifically, this class encompasses the majority of well-known normal implicational logics in a universal setting. The study employs a method of reducing serial complexity order to derive the mentioned results. We demonstrate that each hypersequent logic in the mentioned category has either a relatively simple or undecidable truth-set when its signature is treated as exhaustive. This truth-set complexity imparts both the model completeness and the truth-set filter completeness of its corresponding modal counterpart. Furthermore, we show that each deductively complete hypersequent logic in the mentioned category has either an undecidable decision procedure or is solved undecidably. We present this new classification framework as a set of conditions that can be used to derive the mentioned results. The framework's first condition reveals an intriguing connection between the relative complexity order of languages and foundational logical capabilities, specifically involving the management of constant symbols and variables. The second condition reflects on the effect of rule types on logical processing, especially the interaction of different premisses in deductive reasoning. We illustrate the feasibility of this classification framework through examples of applicability to entire families of hypersequent logics.

This research presents HyperExpan, a novel method for expanding a taxonomic structure through representation learning of hyperbolic embeddings. Unlike existing methods, HyperExpan utilizes an adaptable approach to connect newly introduced concepts to the existing taxonomy in the most efficient way possible. It achieves this without requiring extensive information about the newly integrated concepts or an existing taxonomy. Moreover, HyperExpan can easily update taxonomies by incorporating new concepts while maintaining compliance with the property of ultrametricity. To accomplish this goal, HyperExpan employs a unique and efficient technique that rapidly adapts to new concepts using a combination of fast and heavy sampling approaches. As a result, it consistently achieves superior performance in multiple benchmark tests. Furthermore, HyperExpan's ability to efficiently handle concept additions and rapid adaptation to new concepts makes it well-suited for various real-world applications.

A comprehensive analysis has been conducted to investigate the impact of electric fields on a broad spectrum of molecular interactions, focusing on the calculations of dIB4 values for pairs in the S66 dataset. Calculations were carried out using a host-guest supermolecule approach and Polarizable Continuum Model (PCM), with both approaches being compared to a more advanced method that accounts for interactions with light and the distribution of charge within the molecules. Additionally, the study assesses the accuracy of lower-cost PCM method in predicting interactions and explores the connection between electric field values and molecular orientation in relation to the field.

The fourth Industrial Revolution has brought about a significant shift in manufacturing system design, emphasizing exceptional production services and relentless minimalization of lead times. Achieving these goals requires unprecedented accuracy in lead time predictions, a challenging task when uncertain production times are involved. This study focuses on incorporating stochastic uncertainty into manufacturing system models to facilitate more precise lead time estimates and enhanced performance metrics. Specifically, we investigated the impact of stochastic uncertainty on System Performance Output, a key indicator in Industry 4.0 settings. To derive an analytical expression for this performance metric, we combined theoretical modelling with validated numerical simulations, utilizing data from a real-world machinery operation. Validation involved comparing the results of theoretical modelling with actual data and finding a strong positive correlation between the two. This research offers practical insights and insights that can be applied directly to manufacturing system managers.

Cyber-Physical Systems rely heavily on a specific method to maintain performance under disruptions, which brings its own challenges. There are multiple definitions of resilience that cater to different needs, but they lack a unified approach, making it difficult to integrate resilience features into traditional design processes. This research proposes a framework that tackles resilience at a system-level through a time-dependent approach, using a specific formulation that combines Discrete-Time STL and nonlinear control techniques. The effectiveness of this framework has been demonstrated through a practical application and tested on a multi-layered human-driven system found in transportation systems.

A novel method for detecting dark substances like dark matter and dark radiation is proposed, employing an extensive network of wide-area accelerometers. The feasibility of detecting particle-like and mediators from these networks has been successfully demonstrated. The results show that a substantial number of accelerometers can reach a sensitivity level at which the acceleration due to a dark substance's influence approaches the sensitivity limit of Earth's gravity. The detection range for this scenario corresponds to a radius of approximately $10-\ 100\ \mathrm{pc}$ for particles and up to $10^4\ \mathrm{pc}$ for scalar and vector mediators. Furthermore, a corresponding change in the Earth's rotational energy density has been presented as an alternative detection criterion, which could result in the detection of dark substances even when their density is much lower. The strategy of using an extensive accelerometer network has been found to be the most effective method for detecting dark substances, particularly for scenarios in which their density is much lower than the surrounding density of ordinary matter.

Consider a nonlinear diffusion equation on a complete manifold $M$, where the operator is non-flat but uniformly elliptic. Let $u$ be a solution that belongs to the class $C^{2, \alpha}$. Under sufficient conditions, for any point $p$ on $M$, there exists a finite set $S$ containing only zeros of the gradient of $u$, and a constant $C > 0$, such that for all $s$ in the set $S$, the gradient estimate holds: \[ \nabla_{\gamma} u(p) \approx \frac{\int_M \Phi(x) \nabla_{\gamma} u(x) \,dx}{\int_M \Phi(x) \,dx}, \] where $\Gamma$ is the metric induced by a normal random matrix and $\Phi$ is a computable function independent of $u$.

Radio sources powered by an Active Galactic Nucleus have significant magnetic fields influencing their polarization properties, affecting observations of plasma and contaminating cosmic microwave background measurements. Understanding the polarization-statistics relationship with source characteristics is essential. By analyzing large radio source samples from 1.4 GHz surveys, researchers have calculated the median fractional polarization in sources of varying sizes. To do so, they tracked the decay of the source's polarization as the angular diameter increases, from 10 to 1 milliarcsseconds. Stacking radiomorphs, a measure that accounts for source number density and angular size, yields valuable polarization data. By combining Morphlock's source characterizations with Hammer/Beers source polarization, they found a significant decline in the polarization at larger sizes, correlating with a 95% confidence. Additionally, there was an unexpected increase in the polarization at morphic sizes over 1 arcsecond.

Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) are a type of mathematical model based on Markov processes, but with the critical difference of having an inaccessible internal state, which can only be inferred through an observation process. HMMs were initially introduced to phonetic analysis in the 1970s and have since been applied in various security models as a form of probabilistic protocol analysis. Due to their limitations, HMMs have been extended or replaced by other models, such as probabilistic bisimulation and probabilistic bisimilarity with observations, which allow for the comparison of systems based on their observable behaviour. We're investigating a novel generalization of HMMs, which we call abstract HMMs (ahHMMs). In this model, the results of transitions can be represented as distributions of possible observation lists rather than fixed strings. AhHMMs can serve as a monadic description of a variant of probabilistic non-interacting non-uniform hybrid systems, specifically the HYLO system 'P_NI_HYLO(O)', which combines probabilistic and non-uniform components.

This paper for the first time reveals the underlying statistical basis for the nonlocal effects seen in dynamically consistent beam theories. Formerly, expressions for sectional stiffness and mass per unit length were derived by averaging over the cross-section. Here, we derive an expression for the sectional moment of inertia. By applying the principle of minimum average kinetic energy, we obtain the Coriolis and damping forces. The emergence of energy conservation and the absence of spurious modes in statically indeterminate structures confirms the dynamically consistent framework's validity. Moreover, we demonstrate that the framework has inherent statistical underpinnings, as indicated by the presence of nonlocal terms. To emphasize the framework's practical applicability, we provide an analytical solution for the natural frequencies of a cantilever beam and compare them to experimental and FEM results. The effectiveness of our approach is further shown in a numerical model of a framed structure.

In the flexible scattering phenomenology approach, event shapes and distributions are expressed through the scattering plane's invariant density, which is a function of $t = s \sin^2\theta^{*}$. We analyze the properties of the density function in relation to the underlying scattering amplitude, and derive its sum rules relevant to the real and imaginary components of the amplitude. These sum rules are then applied to the $\gamma^*/Z$ vector form factor, enabling the construction of a convolution formula for the $Z$ event shape distribution. We verify that the proposed phenomenology is compatible with the standard model, and evaluate the predicted $Z$ event shape distribution using Monte Carlo data for hadron colliders. Furthermore, the phenomenology is used to develop an independent, model-independent observables method for extracting the Higgs signal over background ratio in future $e^+e^-\to Zh$ experiments at the ILC.

This paper presents a comprehensive study on the electromagnetic radiation's interaction with a blackbody that is surrounded by Casimir's phenomenon. To achieve this, we develop formulas for the blackbody's spectral and total energy, radiated power, and surface heat flux both with and without considering the effect of Casimir's phenomenon. Furthermore, we establish the general equations of blackbody's spectral and total entropy in the presence of Casimir's influence up to a high temperature level of 1500 K. Consequently, we examine the effect of Casimir's phenomenon on the thermal radiation characteristics of a blackbody in different temperature conditions.

Protecting the privacy of users using location data is a vital concern, 
particularly given the high accuracy of current GPS systems. Current 
standards for measuring and maintaining location-based privacy are 
historically rooted in protecting individual days, while significantly 
lower bounds have been set on secure location data retention periods. 
Despite the development of a standardized framework for assessing location 
privacy risk, measuring location data retention constraints in different 
systems remains an complex issue. This document explores the use of 
conditional probability distributions in the standard location track model 
and derives lower bounds for location data retention, with calculations 
based on the standard and extended Kalman filter models. A simple 
measurement error model is applied, with analysis conducted via both 
dissipation and preservation of privacy. Compared to previous work, these 
results derive lower bounds for location data retention applicable to 
various privacy standards, with a focus on the standard Kalman filter 
model.

A crucial task in robotics and computer vision, 3D point cloud localization, involves determining the position of a partially scanned point cloud in reference to a full scan taken earlier. The issue of point-based scarcity in localization, common in surveys of large indoor spaces with LiDAR, is typically alleviated by employing Normal Distribution Transform (NDT) representation for data compression. Nonetheless, standard single-frame NDPT-based localizers deliver only moderate precision and are not adaptable to real-time, complex settings involving sequential frame associations. To address this shortcoming, a novel method is proposed, using a Transformer-style encoder-decoder network to integrate compressed NDPT features across multiple frames. The proposed NDT-Transformer localizer is evaluated using extensive datasets including real-world scans collected with an automotive LiDAR and comparisons with competing approaches show that it surpasses them in both accuracy and speed.

Recent large-scale databases of resting-state fMRI connectivity have enabled novel applications such as brain network-based diagnosis and forecasting, offering unparalleled opportunities to discover fresh insights from extensively collected data, specifically in the realm of forecasting. We carried out a comprehensive assessment across 16 publicly available multisite fMRI connectivity datasets to determine the precision of individual and combined predictions regarding fMRI connectivity strength. Our investigation identified that the accuracy of predicting strength relies on the specific network or brain region in question; we further found that integrating information from multiple sites can, in fact, enhance the overall prediction accuracy compared to using a single site alone. We believe our research contributes valuable insights to the domain of fMRI connectivity and network forecasting.

This paper presents a single-node optimization approach that leverages network reachability properties to efficiently manage beeping networks and minimize energy consumption. The name assignment method introduced here achieves optimal results for specific scenarios where all nodes share a particular property, and it conserves energy by utilizing an efficient checking process. To validate the efficacy of this approach, we prove that the proposed solution has a superlinear complexity, specifically O(n^(1-2/p)), where p denotes the beeping probability threshold (p = 0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9, 1.0). Moreover, we compare our algorithm's performance to that of a random strategy through comprehensive simulations, finding that this beeping optimization method leads to a notable reduction in beeping activities, with the degree of this reduction found to be proportional to node population size.

Recent advances in NLP for code-mixed texts have gained considerable attention, primarily driven by the widespread use of language blending in social media across multilingual countries such as India, Brazil, and Sudan. Various approaches have been employed to tackle language identity issues and punctuation-dependent positional encoding (PE) methods have also been developed to enhance performance. However, PE-based techniques struggle with predicting punctuation since they are conditional on the previous word's language identity and category. To overcome this limitation, our proposed Switching Point based Adaptive and Relative Positional Encoding (PESTO) model introduces a novel relative PE scheme that determines relevant previous punctuation marks as a soft language identity switch and adapts to words' language identity and category while preserving the crucial information from the previous punctuation marks. The proposed approach is evaluated on notable datasets for code-mixed text, specifically IITP-IND, IND-ENG, and ROMIND, and significantly surpasses the state-of-the-art benchmarks, showcasing a 1.30% improvement in micro-averaged F1-score for the highly mixed IITP-IND dataset, a 0.76% improvement in the moderately mixed ROMIND dataset, and a 3.01% improvement in the low mixed IND-ENG dataset. The research code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/nitaatiit/PESTO-IND.

The way electron density varies near the sulfur $3p$ band's singular point, known as a van Hove singularity (VHS), has been crucial in forecasting how the critical temperature behaves under pressure in recently discovered sulfur hydride superconductors. We used two different many-body approaches to calculate how the critical temperature changes with pressure, one that accounts for VHS and another that does not. Our results show that incorporating VHS in our calculation improves agreement between theory and experiment, and we find that the model that accounts for VHS works as well as a simple model that uses a single energy band. Both models work better than a more complex model that does not account for VHS. We examined the pressure variation of several experimental measures of the critical temperature, such as how the slope at a particular pressure and the curvature at another pressure behave. Our results match experimental findings when we include VHS in our calculation. The success of our simple model that includes VHS suggests we are close to understanding how this superconducting material works.

Real-world environments with dynamic obstacles, such as pedestrians or cars, present a significant challenge for motion planning among mobile robots of various types. To navigate these environments efficiently, a spatial restriction approach can simplify the motion planning problem, turning it into a feasible and efficient process. This method imposes constraints that are easy to comply with, such as keeping a safe distance from obstacles. Our work focuses on generating spatial restrictions for a particular class of problems involving moving obstacles. Unlike existing methods, our approach is grounded in geometry rather than topology and applies to any shape of mobile obstacles. It uses a map of the area and an initial path as references to generate and update spatial restrictions efficiently. Unlike other topological methods, our approach avoids transforming the map or tracking history, making it more scalable for large and dynamic environments. We have tested our approach all over the world with successful results showing our approach matches the other topological methods efficiency wise but outperforms them in terms of processing time and memory requirements.

This research proposes a method for visual relocalization based on geometric information-derived 3D surfel maps. A key feature of our approach is the use of a refined network for improved feature description, paired with a query feature matcher and a 3D template mask. By leveraging a pre-constructed map of 3D surfels, our method supports more accurate relocalization, especially under difficult conditions. Moreover, our method can accommodate the addition of new 3D data to the surfel map without significant negative impact on a GPU. In a comparative assessment, our method outperformed existing state-of-the-art methods with the A2E and Baidu dataset. A detailed explanation of our approach can be found on our project website at the specified location.

In the context of multiuser MIMO, the challenge of determining user selection and precoder design is complex and closely intertwined. To address this issue, a novel optimization method utilizing the LASSO technique has been developed. By incorporating group LASSO into linear regression, this approach simultaneously identifies user selection and precoder design with minimal loss. A key feature of this technique is its ability to apply to both narrowband and wideband systems, the latter of which involves deriving a closed-form solution for user selection. To estimate channel state information at the base station under a high signal power condition, a new technique called activity detection is introduced. A joint optimization method for wideband multiuser MIMO is then proposed, incorporating activity level estimation into the algorithm. To overcome the computational intensity of the LASSO method under a high number of users, an alternative algorithm using orthogonal pursuit has been developed to provide a suboptimal solution. Simulation results confirm the promising performance of the proposed methods.

The values of rational functions on non-singular tropical curves with respect to a given tropical semifield are continuous and vary based on the support and degrees of the functions. It has been continuously proven that a finite collection of tropical functions with disjoint supports can be combined to produce all the values of rational functions on a non-singular tropical curve. Furthermore, we have established that a finite collection of tropical functions with disjoint subsets can be mixed to produce all the rational function values over a given tropical semifield, and this applies universally. We have also found that a non-degenerate polytope's weight system can be produced by a finite combination of its tropical development's weight functions. We have established the feasibility of a algorithmic method that, given a polytope, identifies a finite subset of its tropical development's weight functions that can be combined to produce all the weight functions of the polytope. This algorithmic method was successfully implemented for two given polytopes with specific properties and for rational and max semifields.

We establish that in a particular region of the complex plane, the absolute value of the cumulative distribution function of the standard Gaussian distribution converges uniformly to the Q-function, which is defined as the integral of the standard Gaussian distribution over a particular interval. Additionally, it is observed that in another region of the complex plane, the difference between the cumulative distribution function and the Q-function is either predominantly large, greater than 1/2, or predominantly small, less than 1/2.

It is demonstrated that the Fox-Hatcher one-form combines with a specific iterated integral, derived from a Vassiliev invariant of Novikov type and of order two, to form a form representing a Vassiliev invariant of order three.
