By using this metric, it reduces the complexity of power allocation by eliminating the need for individual interface activation constraints, thereby yielding more optimal results. Furthermore, it develops a semi-closed form solution for power allocation, which provides valuable insights for practical applications. This solution, along with an activation pattern obtained at optimal efficiency, is applied to yield substantial power savings while maintaining satisfactory data transfer rates. A simulated case study demonstrates the efficacy of the proposed joint programming approach, yielding up to 50% reduced power consumption compared to separate optimization of scheduling and power allocation.

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities, such as those found on the surfaces of materials, by accurately modeling the electronic properties of a magnetic impurity and its associated YSR states. Utilizing this established framework, our research examines the electronic properties of individual Mn and Cl-doped Nb atoms on the Nb(110) surface. Our results, derived from intricate many-body calculations, match experimental findings and highlight the intricate interplay between YSR states and the electronic spectrum of the host material. These calculations also assess the feasibility of applying the YSR state technique for detecting isolated magnetic impurities within complex systems.

The NA62 experiment at CERN has published its initial findings on the search for the rare K+ to pi+ neutrino-antineutrino decay, utilizing the decay-in-motion technique. With a sample of 825,000 K+ decays, the experiment has set a world-record sensitivity by observing eight instances. With an estimated branching ratio limit of 0.75 x 10^-10, the results exceed all previous conventions and constraints. Furthermore, the experiment has constrained the electroweak penguin process and the Smith and Voloshin mechanisms, resulting in a range of 2-10 times 10^-7 psi and 2-10 times 10^-8 psi respectively, for relevant model parameters. These findings represent a significant step towards the 10^-10 level sensitivity that the beam dump Cherenkov detector SHiP is expected to achieve.

Distributed simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) requires each agent to construct its own map, leading to potential information sharing between animals, robots, or humans, which may result in map collision when multiple agents create maps simultaneously. Traditional methods attempt to prevent information sharing by assigning unique features to each agent, but in cases of close proximity or with impaired sensory input, these measures can fail. To prevent such map collisions, it's established that the best approach is for all agents to share the same mapping features. To achieve this, past research has proposed the assignment of an invariant feature to each point based on its local geometric structure, but proposed architectures relied on a single, existing feature extraction method which proved ineffective in diverse environments or with impaired sensory input. Our work presents DNNFilter, a neural network-based feature assignment method that's specifically designed to detect edges, which outperforms existing approaches in various scenarios and effectively mitigates bias caused by sensory impairments.

This study focuses on identifying the finer edges within satellite imagery, 
particularly those related to buildings, roads, and vegetation patterns. 
Deep learning techniques are commonly utilized for this purpose, but they 
depend heavily on large datasets, are difficult to adapt and adjust. In 
contrast, our approach draws inspiration from established image processing 
methods, specifically the Laplacian pyramid and Canny edge detection algorithms. 
By integrating these methods in a controlled manner, we successfully extract 
more precise edge detections compared to a pre-trained neural network, 
all without requiring any additional training. Furthermore, our approach 
is highly versatile, as it only requires input from pixel values within a 
given image, and can be influenced by varying two critical parameters, 
allowing for optimal edge detection results.

Just under a decade ago, the emergence of non-linear high fluence X-ray absorption near edge spectroscopy was documented. This phenomenon was primarily observed in dense amorphous materials. A new theoretical model has been developed to accurately simulate this non-linear behavior by analyzing changes in electronic configuration. The one-body approximation model has been implemented to calculate XANES spectra in turbulent electronic environments. The proposed model exhibits reduced saturation levels compared to earlier linear theories, making it more effective. The satiation levels of this model are comparable to those of a previously established saturation theory by Khalkhali et al. and are in alignment with experimental measurements. The proposed model has been successfully applied to two dense glass materials and its validity has been verified through practical analysis.

The application of Deep Neural Networks in Automatic Modulation Classification has shown significant promise, but it is vulnerable to attacks. This research presents an innovative approach called the BlendGAN technique, which combines the capabilities of RealGAN and WGAN to produce a robust and stable classifier that can accurately identify uncertainty and resist adversarial attacks. The effectiveness of the proposed method was demonstrated through experimentation on diverse scatters and mixtures of signals, showing improved performance compared to existing solutions.

Segmentation of Multiple Sclerosis lesions is an issue that experts struggle with.
Recent studies showcase that artificial intelligence can segment these lesions with
precision. Despite this, continuing to train neural networks on existing datasets may
not be cost-effective. This study investigates whether adding variations of a
well-established algorithm can continuously improve performance without retraining,
especially in scenarios where labels from prior studies are used. We extended
the $n$^th$ Order U-Net model, a recent top-performing multiple sclerosis lesion
segmentation algorithm, by incorporating two sources of information: adjusting
the data and incorporating classification of ground glass lesions. Our findings
indicate that continuous improvement is effective in achieving high segmentation
precision without retraining the original model, especially when incorporating
classification of ground glass lesions has additional benefits.

The 2022 edition of the ISIB conference, held in Paris, brought together
leading experts in the fields of statistical physics, Informatics, and
mathematics to share the most recent advancements. The presented research
focused on understanding complex systems, analyzing complex data, and exploring
at the intersection of theoretical and applied sciences. This publication
consists of a lightly edited version of the presented papers.

A straightforward framework has been created to predict when mathematical models make errors when simulating complex systems with non-repeating patterns, such as weather or the movement of birds. This method uses a separate model to analyze the long-term behavior of these systems and identifies turning points where their behavior may shift unexpectedly. Since these points often occur at nearly identical states with slight differences, this task is well-suited for solution using machine learning that can identify patterns in complex data, such as the movement of birds. For instance, if a model simulating the movement of birds predicts that the birds will fly into each other based on their recent trajectory, this method can be used to identify the mistake and suggest a more likely prediction with similar likelihood. This framework has been developed based on analyzing simple systems with repeating patterns, which facilitated the creation of a new approach for simulating these systems that incorporates error detection. For systems without repeating patterns, such as the movement of birds, this method involves using two models to simulate the long-term behavior of these systems and identifies turning points where their behavior may diverge differently based on slight differences in initial conditions. By combining these approaches, this framework can simulate complex systems and detect potential mistakes with confidence metrics.

The evolution of massive star formation (MSF) cores is significantly influenced by the suppression of turbulent fragmentation within the surrounding environment. Observations of molecular emission toward MSF cores typically provide an average perspective, but a lack of data on the cores' interior means we can't fully understand how they form. To bridge this knowledge gap, we conducted a high-resolution survey of the 1.3 mm continuum in the Dragon infrared dark cloud, a known hub-filament system hosting several MSF cores. Our research revealed the presence of extensive, large-scale outflow and shock signatures from the core's expansion, most notably from the core L1162B. Within this core, we found a significant (1.7 mag) color temperature variation, consistent with the core's center being expanding at 1000 au while the edges remain relatively cold (~10 K). These unique findings correlate with the core's incorporation of falls, which have brought ~10$^3$ M_\odot of material toward its center, accompanied by significant dynamical effects. We conclude that this behavior indicates successful formation of massive stars, driven by the core's interior and exterior dynamical states.

A new computational tool, PopSyCLE, is used to determine the range of values for Primordial Black Hole masses that could account for Dark Matter based on varying particle collision probabilities. The tool's input includes specifications for the primary particle collision channels and their corresponding probabilities. Three different models of particle collisions are employed in the calculations: monopole-only, standard non-gravitational, and total (including standard non-gravitational and gravitational), each with varying probabilities. The resulting plots illustrate how the intensity of particle collisions impacts the range of values for Primordial Black Hole masses that could account for Dark Matter.

We utilize molecular dynamics simulations to examine a system consisting of virtual wedges formed by spherical particles, where each wedge represents an irregular hexagon with evenly spaced facets. The objective is to investigate how these virtual wedges modulate their facets in a manner similar to chiral nematic liquid crystals that exhibit polarization modulation. The existence of both first and higher-order modulations in the system is validated through simulations of varying system sizes, pressures, and particle polydispersity. The results indicate that the first-order modulations persist across the studied conditions, whereas higher-order modulations are only observed under specific ranges of pressure and dispersion. Additionally, we analyze how the observed modulation patterns change depending on the angle between adjacent wedges in the system.

Recent advancements in the NLP field have been rapidly adopting large pre-trained language models. While these models provide outstanding performance when fine-tuned for specific tasks, their large size hinders their practical application on various platforms. To overcome this limitation, research has focused on developing more efficient methods for model fine-tuning. Our study introduces a novel parameter-efficient model adjustment strategy, which incorporates special tokens to enhance the efficiency of model updates. Our proposed algorithm allows the model to achieve high performance with minimal modifications, as updates can be performed at the token level, and optimization algorithms can be integrated with the model training. Additionally, we examined the potential for leveraging the power of multiple GPUs in model update operations, and our results confirm that this approach can significantly reduce the cost per update, especially when performed on high-performance hardware. Our experiments provide evidence of the success of this update strategy, as it enables model adjustments with just 5% of the original parameters while maintaining or improving performance in most cases across various tasks.

This paper investigates a complex additive preference problem with a context-dependent element of uncertainty. Three distinct context instances are identified - a non-contextual scenario, a moderate context setting with partial information, and a highly uncertain context with limited data availability. Researchers compared two models, a non-contextual baseline method and a contextual preference ordering approach (CPO), to determine which one performs better in each context. It was found that the CPO method produces better rankings in both moderate and highly uncertain contexts. Further, the CPO method's ability to utilize context information was demonstrated through its interaction with a variety of uncertainty levels, thus enabling it to tackle more challenging situations more effectively. Ultimately, the CPO method's superior performance suggests it as a promising starting point for the development of new context-dependent multi-objective decision-making approaches.

Our investigation explores thermodynamic properties in the light of dynamic behavior for two polymer fluids that exhibit sluggish dynamics. By collecting precise calorimetric data on poly(ethylene oxide) and poly(methyl methacrylate) in interaction with solvents, melt fragility and transition temperatures are determined. Subsequently, using simulations and measuring density fluctuations, the entropic component of the heat capacity is calculated, thereby isolating the caloric contribution. Furthermore, using the ideas from steps-like temperature-dependent specific heat curves as a phase transition model of dynamics and thermodynamics, the observations are analyzed. It is discovered that the dynamic behavior, as described by non-Newtonian dynamics of relativity low frequencies, can be well correlated with the temperature dependence of the heat capacity in the vicinity of the glass transition point. Notably, this relationship remains valid even at temperatures far from the glass transition. Hence, the ideas presented here offer a unified description of dynamics and thermodynamics near the glass transition point, thus tackling the challenge of modeling dynamics from thermodynamic data and bridging the gap between these two seemingly unrelated properties in glass-forming materials.

Human language utilizes various forms of rejection such as negation and negating verbs to convey denial or negation. Previous studies on artificial neural networks have concentrated on learning patterns within natural language, without by design incorporating mechanisms for rejecting or denying information. In this study, we examine the capacity of Transformer-based language models to automatically learn rejection mechanisms during training, focusing on their ability to differentiate between true and false information and incorporate not-knowing responses in their output. We introduce two novel metrics to assess a model's rejection performance: (i) truth denial accuracy, measuring its ability to correctly deny true information, and (ii) information gap accuracy, evaluating its ability to appropriately not know or remain silent in the presence of unknown information. We apply these metrics to four diverse models, including the well-known BERT, ILVQ, and the two variants of Transformer-XL, each of which exhibits varying degrees of contextual understanding and different design priorities. We discover that only ILVQ displays a healthy truth denial performance, with BERT exhibiting over-reliance on denying information and information gap performance varying significantly across models. These results imply that rejecting or denying information is a highly complex task, requiring sophisticated models like ILVQ to perform effectively.

To improve decision making, consider looking ahead at potential outcomes. 
This study investigates the effect of a specifically designed "look-ahead" strategy 
in the decoding process of Neural Machine Translation. By anticipating the 
translations of subsequent sentences, we develop an approach that focuses on relevant words in the source text. Our strategy combines a source side focus mechanism with a novel look-ahead attention that aggregates predictions from various sentences. Theoretical analysis and experiments on 7 major language pairs demonstrate that this strategy enhances translation accuracy and is influenced by the number of looked-ahead sentences. Interestingly, one-way symmetric aggregation of look-ahead contexts yields high performance, suggesting that ambiguous source information is resolved as more relevant sentences are considered.

This passage uses a structured approach to calculate the Kontsevich weights for the graphs related to connection and curvature definitions within a formal symplectic framework. A key structural discovery was that a weighted transformation over a 2d manifold M can be expressed as a sum of two structured terms. Furthermore, weight assignments for the terms provide explicit formulas for the connection and curvature graphs, enabling generalizations to arbitrary finite-dimensional vector spaces.

This research investigates the dynamics of an $\mathcal{N} =4$ supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory in the large $N$ limit across a broad spectrum of 't Hooft couplings, where the thermal phase is compared to the entanglement phase. It's long been acknowledged that when the 't Hooft coupling varies between zero and infinity, the N=4 SYM theory develops a holographic dual in time-dependent frame, whose classical dynamics yields a simple solution. However, when the coupling exceeds a specific threshold, the N=4 SYM theory enters a non-thermal stage, whose properties are largely unknown yet intriguing, as it's thought to be an instance of an interacting conformal field theory. Our work reveals that when the thermal and entanglement phases are compared, the N=4 SYM theory follows a predictable pattern, supporting prior research, yet when compared solely to itself, the theory exhibits a intricate relationship between its thermal behavior and 't Hooft coupling. Our research, complemented by mathematical calculations from Kaloper and Qiu, demonstrates that when the thermal and entanglement phases are examined in detail, the N=4 SYM theory adheres to a predictable structure, supported by analytical solutions at specific points within the theory. It's these solutions that unlock a broad understanding of the theory's dynamics, encompassing its dynamics across a broad spectrum of 't Hooft couplings, leading to new findings regarding entanglement entropy

This paper seeks to build upon the framework developed by Zhang et al. to price Asian options, previously published in a 2020 paper. We aim to address the gaps identified in the framework as outlined by Artzner,anka, and Chen in their 2022 research. We introduce new results within the context of a geometric Brownian motion, a model commonly used in financial literature. These outcomes offer a comprehensive set of axioms leading to a coherent pricing theory for Asian options quoted as a fixed rate or a volume. The study also investigates the relationship between the option seller and buyer, calculating losses and gains for both parties in different scenarios. In addition, we extend the pricing framework developed by Zhang et al. to include backward dynamic programming and apply it to a dividend-paying geometric Brownian motion.

The universe's large-scale distribution of dark matter influences the formation of galaxies and their physical properties. Observations of galaxy clusters indicate they harbor significant, yet previously unknown, amounts of dark matter. For this reason, scientists are particularly interested in the implications of dark matter's presence in galaxy clusters, especially its potential to produce radiation at the gamma-ray frequency. Earlier studies suggested that dark matter within galaxies might give rise to a detectable gamma-ray signal at the level of millijanskies ($10^{-3}$mJy) in the near-earth astronomical context. however, this research focused solely on the radiation produced by baryons and dark matter within galaxies, disregarding potential contributions from galaxy clusters. we propose to study the combined effect of gamma-ray radiation from galaxies and galaxy clusters within a $10^{16}$ M$\blacksquare$ distance range on near-earth observatories, taking into account data from the Fermi Large Area Telescope. by applying the runge-kutta method to numerically analyze the diffusion and dispersion of dark matter particles, this research calculates their likely impact on galaxy spectra and estimates that the combined radiation from galaxies and galaxy clusters may account for up to $10\%$ of the observed discrete gamma-ray flux.

We investigate the cosmological collision of two extremely massive particles or fields, discovering that their classical interaction can lead to distinct anomalies in the cosmic abundance of primordial power, possibly fitting observations better than standard models. These anomalies may originate from a variety of classical collisions involving multiple fields, either separately or combined. Evidence for these features is found in the distinct patterns of breaking and combination of symmetry as well as the mixing of quanta from different fields, with the possibility of detecting them through projections on specific models, including the Galileon and massive gravity frameworks. These features, if they exist, could offer new insights into the early universe, expanding our understanding of cosmological interaction and possibly opening up new avenues of cosmological research.

Understanding how complex visual models work is crucial, and developing techniques to explain these models can be challenging due to their highly non-linear nature. We propose a straightforward explanation mechanism for any existing convolutional neural network (CNN) that works with any input image, without needing to modify its architecture. Our method, called LVFF, uses a pre-trained network to generate an image that represents the network's interpretation of the input, by combining specific filter components. The extracted image shows the network's focus, allowing users to measure the level of confidence and accuracy. Additionally, by using a learned mapping, users can translate image regions to meaningful human understandings. We tested LVFF on several tasks, including detecting Adversarial Examples and identifying Rationale for Classification Decisions.

The interaction between transverse optical phonons and electrons plays a key role in cuprate one-dimensional (1D) materials, leading to a direct coupling between their energies. This phonon-electron coupling in 1D materials gives rise to a long-range attraction forces between ions connected by this transverse phonon. Utilizing a rigorous numerical approach, we address the challenge of paired transverse phonons in a long, finite chain, ultimately obtaining a potential resembling a repulsive hard-core 1D gas model, especially when the phonon Debye wave number is high. However, we observe a slight discrepancy, approximately 3%, from the predicted ground state energy for a repulsive hard-core 1D gas model, based on numerical calculations by van Konynenburg and Christ. Furthermore, we investigate the normal mode spectra of two coupled, short 1D chains via density-matrix renormalization group calculations, revealing a significant decrease in a low-frequency mode as a measure of its dispersion relationship, when the phonon Debye wave number is high.

This study implements a discovery learning algorithm in a simulated healthcare environment. A causal structural discovery algorithm is used to analyze dummy individual healthcare data. Learning objectives are set, a causal graph is inferred, and the impact of the resulting model is evaluated. Discovery learning results in a model that simulates healthcare decision making. This decision is then utilized for hypothetical risk management decisions.

A magnet with a certain composition, specifically Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$, has been found to display properties of topological melting and chiral symmetry breaking at temperatures and biases within a specific range. This specific range sits within a broader window of stability, within which the material forms a regular, ordered pattern of "skyrmion" structures, typically observed using a scanning tunneling microscope under controlled environmental conditions. Our investigation of the system's properties, combined with a detailed computational analysis, allows for a complete understanding of the material's phase transitions and shows that the skyrmion structure begins to destabilize well before it loses its stability and collapses. This particular behavior has significant implications for searches of any magnetic analogues to exotic particles such as quarks and gluons.

High-dimensional data streams are becoming increasingly common in numerous fields of study. A variety of statistical models have been developed to analyze such data frames, which often feature a small number of key variables within a large set of secondary variables. These frames exhibit different characteristics, particularly in terms of the temporal nature and presence of key variables, leading to the introduction of dynamic models that incorporate time trends and variable interactions. This overview focuses on a selection of models tailored for high-dimensional data frames, particularly highlighting their applications, implementations, and underlying assumptions. This survey aims to provide in-depth insights into the main ideas and will serve as a resource for understanding the complexities involved; it also highlights areas of improvement and introduces novel research avenues for further exploration.

The equilibrium problem described by Nikaido-Okada and Almeida et al. has been widely used in the study of variational inequalities and equilibrium problems. This paper aims to provide a clear demonstration of how the fixed point method can be applied to solve the Nikaido-Okada equilibrium problem and an associated variational inequality. Additionally, we will present an example to illustrate the relevance of the iterative sequences in the context of a monotone variational inequality.

In the realm of multimedia security, secure data concealment is an emerging concept, enabling the gradual disclosure of data while preserving privacy. This research focuses on a more challenging variation of this issue, using reversible concealment to extract essential details from encrypted messages. Our proposed solution involves a pair of network components - a reversible proxy and a Bayesian transformer - that work in tandem to extract meaningful data from an encrypted input, utilizing a novel inverse reconstruction model based on Bayesian theory. The results of our experiments demonstrate the superior performance of our proposed approach over existing non-reversible concealment methods.

The modeling of turbulent effects in mean-field dynamo models of planetary and stellar convective dynamos is commonly based on an approximation that incorporates only a limited range of turbulent fluctuations.  In this study, we examine whether this approximation is sufficient for accurately accounting for turbulent effects by conducting simulations of global convective dynamos in the presence of varying magnetic fields.  We find that while a simplified model of turbulent effects can successfully reproduce the main characteristics of convective dynamos, it consistently underestimates the strength of magnetic activity exhibited in these simulations.  In particular, the simplified model frequently fails to generate sufficient helicity to account for observed magnetic field geometry, further indicating the need for more comprehensive turbulent modeling.  We subsequently perform additional simulations that incorporate a more complete representation of turbulent effects, which is based on a comprehensive spectrum of turbulent fluctuations.  We find, however, that even with this enhanced representation of turbulent effects, simulations that account for energy transport losses and those that do not draw approximately the same magnetic field morphology.  We propose that this outcome may be attributed to the existence of multiple stable dynamo regimes in convective dynamos, with rapid rotation playing a key role in the stabilization of these dynamo operations.

The flow of gas and molecules in the central area of the galaxy NGC4945 has been thoroughly examined using compact imaging technology at a frequency of 345.9 GHz. Data collected demonstrate an intricate molecular pattern consisting of a primary circular area approximately 3.53 parsecs in diameter and a secondary, less concentrated region about 5 to 7 parsecs away from the galaxy's core. Specifically, the secondary region includes a substantial, faint molecular spiral arm that runs perpendicular to the galaxy's main axis. An examination of line ratios suggests that this molecular spiral arm is likely the result of core expulsion due to the galaxy's vertical axis disruption. Such a core expulsion event may also be responsible for a 40,000 solar mass star cluster, as well as highly abundant ratios of 13C/12C and 16O/14O in the galaxy's core. However, the ratios are similar to those observed in the galaxy's disk, particularly in the second molecular spiral arm.

A novel solver has been developed for a computational framework recently proposed to study plasma dynamics in magnetized systems over extended periods of time. The inbuilt quasilinear diffusion model helps maintain stability of the solver in simulations where the density distribution changes significantly, thereby preventing simulations from becoming unstable and inaccurate. The solver incorporates a fully conservative particle-in-cell algorithm with multiple species and electromagnetic simulations, designed in a modular way to facilitate easy integration with additional kinetic models based on the Fokker-Planck formalism. The newly developed simulator has the ability to simulate scenarios ranging from small-scale to large-scale systems, offering a high level of precision and efficiency through the implementation of unsplit higher-order finite element methods. Examples of practical applications of the simulator have been presented, including simulations of various plasma dynamics, such as the development of instabilities and particle relaxation processes within magnetized plasmas.

Previous variable stepsize Second Derivative General Linear Methods have already been implemented using the Nordsieck technique, and we extend this work by directly introducing variable stepsize SGLMs onto non-uniform grids. We then establish order conditions for these new methods of order p with q=p stage order and demonstrate them through specific examples up to order four, further confirming their efficiency in solving non-stiff problems via numerical experiments and theoretical convergence analysis.

This paper explores the relationship between the exponential stability of a C0-semigroup T(t) and the positivity of a Lyapunov equation in a Banach space. Under certain conditions, we establish that if there exists a positive, bounded, and continuously differentiable function V(x) with certain properties, such that the function L(T(t), V(x)) is dominated by V(x) multiplied by a converging function C(t), then the semigroup T(t) is exponentially stable. This main finding is further bolstered by numerous applications to various linear and nonlinear evolution equations, as well as their corresponding abstract forms.

MuMuPy is a software application designed to determine the interaction between dimuonium and various substances within a specified environment. It utilizes numerical solutions to the Schrödinger equation along with Kenyon-Brown potential to simulate these interactions. MuMuPy includes an option to graph the results in a three-dimensional format and offers a range of preset options for simulating different conditions. Additionally, the software provides access to the source code, allowing for customization and extension of its functionality. MuMuPy includes a graphical user interface and is available for download at no cost, making it easily accessible to users. It has also been made available on various platforms, including the repository of the Institute of Physics, the Czech Academy of Sciences, and as a ready-to-use virtual machine on SiteHome. A detailed guide to using MuMuPy has been included on SiteHome as well.

Portfolio management professionals face two core issues: determining the optimal asset allocation for a portfolio and predicting future performance. While utility functions can address these problems, typical applications rely on relative values of assets, neglecting the actual performance. This paper integrates both perspectives by developing a utility function that combines absolute and relative values. This model's parameters can be optimized through the two-step Mean-Variance procedure. Although using two separate models for absolute and relative values minimizes complexity, it results in a higher number of models to analyze. Our solution aims to mitigate this drawback and offers a simpler, yet efficient method for analyzing the absolute performance of assets. Additionally, a joint model is proposed, combining absolute and relative values with a new utility function, thereby reducing the need for multiple models and simplifying the analysis process.

Using the presence of IGM absorption in star-forming dwarf galaxy spectra, researchers are studying the galactic wind dynamics and the gravitational potential of these galaxies. By analyzing the strengths of absorption lines from 11 such galaxies, a correlation is established between the potential's shallowest point and the galaxy's rotation velocity. Furthermore, data on the galactic outflow velocities, which range from 70 to 190 km/s, indicate that dwarf galaxies have faster outflows than larger galaxies. Simulation results confirm that the observed outflow velocities are a consequence of the IGM's counter-inflow, and that the deeper gravitational potential of dwarf galaxies allows the IGM to insert a greater velocity relative to the galactic wind. While the IGM's influence often lacks substantial impacts on larger galaxy outflow velocities, it may have a similar effect, albeit on the net flow rather than the accretion rate as simulations have previously suggested.

We investigate how fermionic quasiparticles behave when coupled to a local oscillator through a shared coupling constant. When this oscillator is classical in nature, the corresponding fermionic quasiparticle exhibits an unusual collapse near its ground state for any value of the coupling constant. In contrast, the response of the fermionic quasiparticle to the oscillator when it is quantized shows an unusual turn-up or turn-down in the excitation spectrum for any strength of the coupling constant, occurring either below or above the quasiparticle's energy and potentially affecting its ground state. These unusual properties provide a distinctive signature that can be used to identify unconventional many-body states in systems that are weakly coupled to entropic environments. Additionally, the presence of a local oscillator that is both interacting with the fermionic quasiparticle and influenced by it generates a complex that is similar in form to the polaron. However, there is one distinct difference: whereas the quasiparticle's ground state has experienced an unusual collapse, its excited states exhibit an unusual spread out when compared with the corresponding ground state of the classical polaron.

Golan and Sapir \cite{GS} discovered that the Thompson's groups $F$, $T$, and $V$ exhibit non-elementary limsup limsup divergence. This research extends to $G$-thick groups by constructing examples with every form of limdiv divergence. Furthermore, for the braided Thompson groups, it was shown that $F_b$, $T_b$, and $V_b$ respectively display $F_b$, T_b, and V_b limdiv divergence. Using Golan and Sapir's \cite{GS} method, the findings are also extended to the braided generalized Thompson groups under specific assumptions.

This project involves utilizing the Complete RAG architecture, which incorporates both Retrieval and Generation components, to address the question-answering task. The complete architecture merges the performance of pre-trained models trained in isolation on this task. To achieve this, we demonstrate the effectiveness of an initial model trained without tuning and with minimal adjustments, which significantly reduces the carbon footprint associated with its development. Additionally, a series of experiments was conducted to streamline the model's design and optimize its training hyperparameters, leading to the identification of the best configuration. A thorough evaluation was then performed to assess the model's performance, which resulted in exceptional results, marking a new benchmark in question-answering performance.

This study examines the long-term behavior of the roots and polynomials connected to a specific type of weight function that is logarithmically connected to the distance from the endpoint of the interval. Initially, the investigation focuses on weights that have singularities at the interval boundaries. Later, the analysis broadens to weights without singularities, instead concentrating on the weights' behavior at the interval boundaries. In all these cases, the long-term behavior of the orthogonal polynomials is consistent with the Riesz-Herglotz functional, which describes a specific type of meromorphic function.

Crowdsourcing with Amazon's MTurk has become a popular tool for researchers and industry professionals to obtain data and learn valuable insights. One crucial phase in planning MTurk research involves demographically recruiting participants, but existing studies show that only 60% of announced demonstrations and 18% of announced studies demonstrate actual task submission, indicating a significant problem. With many potential workers available, it is challenging to identify and engage an adequate number of qualified participants, leading to a crowd that lacks diversity and quality, and therefore, researchers face significant obstacles in gathering qualified data. Through an analysis of 525 MTurk demonstrations, we examine the role of demographics in participant recruitment, evaluate best practices, and explore methods to improve engagement, ultimately aiming to assist researchers in effectively utilizing crowd-sourcing for their MTurk research.

Recent text-clipping retrieval research focuses primarily on developing powerful learning models that can effectively match text and clips. This paper introduces TS2-Net, a novel transformer network that incorporates token shift and selection mechanisms to enhance text-clip matching. By incorporating token shift to enhance representation learning, we achieve improved performance. Additionally, our method involves selecting and combining clip tokens and text tokens to optimize final results. The token selection mechanism aligns with human cognition, utilizing attention to key words and phrases that convey primary meanings. This allows our model to effectively handle both dense and sparse data representation. Extensive experimentation on text-clip retrieval benchmarks demonstrates that TS2-Net surpasses current state-of-the-art models with superior performance.

The concept of flavour change caused by neutral currents in the top quark sector is explored, based on an underlying model (BLMTCM), in which top quark flavour changes are facilitated through favourable flavour arrangements involving colourless exchange to maintain a consistent flavour profile. This results in the first observation of taste-changing neutral currents in top colour assisted mechanisms. The associated flavour changing currents are compared to those present in the Standard Model, specifically the CKM matrix, with an emphasis on their differential effects and a method for detection outlined. The interpretation of flavour anomalies, such as the anomalies in W boson mass and bottom quark flavour changing decays, within the BLMTCM framework is also presented.

In our research, we introduce a new class of graph models called directed hybrid random graphs. These graphs are characterized by a small percentage of preferential attachment nodes that attract most of the incoming edges, while the rest of the nodes have a more uniform relationship. We investigate the properties of these directed hybrid random graphs under different attachment probabilities and create mathematical models to quantify their behavior. Our research shows that even a slight preference in attachment can result in a small set of preferential attachment nodes dominating the network and governing the directed hybrid random graphs' behavior. Additionally, we found that the number of unattached edges in directed hybrid random graphs follows a Poisson distribution and that the sum of the outdegrees of all nodes is roughly two times the number of nodes in the network. Finally, our research reveals that the outdegree distribution follows a broken power law, with a mix of exponential and power law distributions.

The proliferation of wireless systems, encompassing wireless networks, has led to a significant increase in electromagnetic radiation. These wireless emissions adversely affect the operation of sensitive equipment, prompting the need for anomaly detection in industrial settings. Traditional detection methods are inadequate, as they can only identify single anomalies or part of a scene that deviates from normal operation. In contrast, wireless disturbance identification necessitates the detection of multiple anomalies or entire scenes exhibiting distortion. To address this, a deep learning approach is proposed for multi-label anomaly detection in wireless disturbance identification. A convolutional neural network architecture has been developed that simultaneously identifies and localizes anomalies in scenes, utilizing a novel dataset, DLWDI. The efficacy of this approach has been demonstrated by comparing it with established classification techniques, yielding an impressive 93.0% accuracy, 0.81465 Pascal value, and 0.9996 F1-measure on the test set of the DLWDI dataset.

To grasp the impact of gravitational forces on both quantum systems moving at varying speeds and stationary particles, we must rely on accurate quantum mechanics theories. This project involves rectifying the inaccuracies in previous quantum mechanics models, which oversimplified complex gravitational effects as linear defects in spacetime. This paper achieves that by rectifying one such model for both moving and stationary particles, incorporating a quantum charge and nonlinear electrodynamics into the Som-Raychaudhuri cosmic string spacetime model featuring linear defects. This revised quantum mechanics model yields significant findings, including a precise explanation for how gravitational forces affect quantum systems and stationary particles. The resulting precise quantum relations for both moving and stationary particles show a complex interplay between displacement, vorticity, and entropy, as well as correlations between charge and energy.

In a particular category of measure algebra structures, we're able to provide a complete description of the locally usual type. A measure algebra is characterized as locally usual if it meets the condition that the set of regulated measures, which correspond to locally regulated functions, holds a significant proportion within the entire space of measures on a particular topological space. Our primary approach involves reducing the general case to a simpler special instance. Our special instance relies on a particular property of countable matchbox permutation games. Additionally, we're also identifying new examples of measure algebras that exhibit unique properties.

Parton distributions that account for quark and gluon correlations in a proton can be understood more clearly through detailed analysis of electron-proton deep inelastic scattering (EPS) experiments that incorporate complex polarized electron beams.  The Hermeticity of Compton scattering (HCS) process, which occurs in addition to standard tensor polarization, can also offer insight into this matter.  However, an alternative new indicator has been suggested, which makes use of the recoiling proton's polarization in the collision.  Our analysis, which uses established target quantities in relation to virtual photon distributions, reveals that this new indicator is distinct from existing ones and offers a significant advantage in studying parton distributions that account for quark and gluon correlations in a proton.  Specifically, it offers a specific example of what could be achieved with the CEBAF detector at Jefferson Lab.  An additional advantage of this new indicator is that it could be measured as early as the 12 GeV operating period, long before the proposed electron ionizer can be used to study the EPS process.

All levels of industry, science, and technology are being transformed by artificial intelligence (AI), which is expanding at an rapid rate. The integration of digital technologies, including AI, has given rise to a new form of intelligence known as augmented synthetic intelligence (ASI). ASI refers to intelligence amplified through a synergistic combination of digital and non-digital components, such as human expertise and resources, to achieve optimized outcomes. By merging these sources in an interactive and balanced way, ASI can effectively address the most complex and challenging problems, utilizing complementary digital and human capabilities to achieve maximum efficiency. This paper will concentrate on defining ASI and outlining a conceptual framework to illustrate its functioning. Additionally, it highlights key applications and forecasts for ASI, emphasizing its potential to drive future developments.

Our research involves exploring the thermal behavior of a novel type of superfluid with stripes, comprised of bosons with significant spin-orbit interactions and linked in a lattice structured in a triangle. The presence of spin-orbit interactions triggers a shift from conventional mean-field descriptions towards a more regenerative, self-correcting approach. As we investigate the interplay of these two effects, we discover two crucial moments in the evolution of the striped superfluid: the point at which order and the presence of vortices intersect, and the second critical threshold marking the disappearance of the striped pattern. Through both theoretical reflection and computer simulation, we have detailed the underlying processes governing these transformations and computed the associated phase transitions within the context of the study's relevant parameters.

Consider a finite abelian group $G$ of order $d$ and rank $r$, representing a product of $r$ groups of orders $p_i^{k_i}$ where $p_i$ are prime numbers. We can construct a graph $G_{G}$ with vertices $\mathbb Z_d / \mathbb Z_{p_1^{k_1}} \times \ldots \times \mathbb Z_d / \mathbb Z_{p_r^{k_r}}$ as the direct product of $r$ cyclic groups, connected by edges if there's a non-zero element $g$ in $G$ such that the product of its components is $p_i$ for each vertex $x_i$. The study of these graphs includes investigating their properties, model realizations, and relationships. Based on the degree of model realizations, a different type of graph degeneracy is defined and used to identify key characteristics, such as the essential components and spanning tree counts. Additionally, non-isomorphic graphs corresponding to unique groups of a given order have been identified, representing half of all possible graphs with up to 16 vertices in this order.

We investigate the AdS/CFT correspondence in low-dimensional AdS_2 and AdS_3 backgrounds derived from Type IIA Quotient quantum mechanics. By examining the monopole operators of the 2d CFT, we discover that their masses are tied to the masses of the corresponding 0d CFT. This enables us to establish a universal correspondence between the 2d CFT and the AdS_2 sector of the 5d CFT. Furthermore, by considering dyon operators in the 3d CFT, we find that their masses are connected to the masses of the dyons within the 0d CFT, based on an exception field formulation of the U(1)_F part of the 5d theory. This allows us to establish a correspondence between the 3d CFT and the AdS_3 sector of the 5d CFT, even though the 't Hooft operator does not map directly to the 3d flavor. The exceptional structure of the U(1)_F sector suggests a new method for introducing a chemical potential into the 5d system, which may potentially revive the study of AdS/CFT correspondence in low-dimensional spaces.

In deep Gaussian process (GP) regression, the suitable GP kernel is of paramount importance. We present a framework that translates elementary mathematical expressions into effective GP kernels. This development enables us to derive new GP kernels that capture inputs with mixed data types and create models that accurately predict performance across entire parameter spaces. Our proposed approach combines symbolic and numerical methods to provide a user-friendly tool for determining appropriate GP kernels, thus streamlining the process for experts and non-experts alike. As a significant bonus, the expressed kernels allow for effortless derivation of their parameterized forms, facilitating inverse inference, i.e., inferring model parameters from observed data within these spaces. We evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed technique on various synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating its superiority to other well-established kernels. This method can be utilized via a Python library called GaPy, which is implemented using the numerical computation tools provided by PyMC3 and Scipy, and is freely available for use.

This paper compares and evaluates potential methods for lessening beam-induced Parity Nonconserving (PNC) interference at future high-energy muon colliders. Strategically choosing the path for the muon beam after it leaves the ionizer, based on its longitudinal position, can significantly affect observations of PNC effects. A new approach utilizing a fast electrical switch to manage the beam line has the potential to greatly enhance sensitivity to extremely weak interactions, particularly in searches for the neutrino mixing between different flavor groups.

We introduce a novel technique for introducing and managing sparsity in neural networks, which leverages the concept of clamped optimal transport. By combining the Sinkhorn-Knopp algorithm with a soft constraint, this method ensures that a significant portion of a distribution's mass is allocated to specific locations on a target domain. This approach aligns with the large-body transport theorem and possesses well-documented mathematical properties, making it suitable for use in machine learning frameworks. We adapt this technique for neural network implementation and conduct a set of experiments to showcase its effectiveness in managing sparsity and facilitating model sharing across related tasks.

According to the Hohenberg-Kohn theorem, magnetization in a solid can be eliminated through external fields with a sufficiently high frequency, but this does not necessarily mean that an effective magnetization cannot be achieved through combinations of low-frequency magnetic fields and other interactions.  In the absence of spin-exchange interactions, a gas of spin-1/2 bosons in a harmonic potential exhibits no inherent obstruction to spinning states, but with the introduction of spin-exchange interactions, a phenomenon emerges in which the gas cannot be magnetized by a single, low-frequency magnetic field.  This is an unusual interaction, with no analogies found in the study of magnetic materials, and it is classified as an 'emergent Pauli obstruction'.  In the presence of spin-exchange interactions, an emergent van Alphen effect is also observed, where individual Landau orbits exhibit features of both spin-singlet and spin-triplet superfluids, depending on the strength of the interaction, and the components of the superfluid exhibit distinct behavior, with one being stable in a particular state near full polarization and the other being stable over a range of states, including a fully polarized state, with a width that scales as the square root of the coupling constant.

The presence of test smells in code is a common occurrence, causing potential risks for software systems. To grasp the magnitude of this problem, researchers examined the views of software developers on the gravity of test smells in actual testing settings. A comprehensive questionnaire distributed to the testing community gathered data on the perceived severity of test smells as perceived by software developers. Over 170 developers participated in the study, providing their opinions on 20 test smells and the impact they have on test effectiveness, effort, and overall quality. The results revealed that according to software developers, test effectiveness is typically affected first, followed by test effort, and then overall quality, consistent across the majority of test smells. This study further categorized the test smells into three groups: those having a limited and minor influence, and those potentially posing significant risks for test quality.

This paper introduces a nonconvex version of the integro-differential brushing process, a type of statistical model used for analyzing discrete data collected on a continuum. The new, nonconvex formulation offers a way to generate pure point processes, essentially "brushing up" the classical Poisson process. The proposed method can be applied in two ways, either through the use of "unattainable" conditions, or by incorporating “unachievable” additional processes into the model. A detailed analysis, along with statistical inference and model selection procedures, is provided for the new, nonconvex IgP, including the development of a unified rank-based test. A range of simulated and real-world datasets are used to demonstrate the effectiveness of this new method.

We introduce the updated version of the KKMCee event generator, which includes both theoretical and experimental Monte Carlo tools for simulating electron-positron, muon-antimuon, and quark-antiquark pair creation in future lepton colliders. This event generator, specifically tailored for the linear collider, complements the KKMCee event generator by incorporating Monte Carlo simulations for the electron-positron process. This integrated tool is essential for developing new physics scenarios and final state simulations for the CLIC and ILC colliders. Users can access the event generator's latest version, version 07.7.04, along with extensive documentation at the official CERNSPCL software repository, and this event generator's contribution at the iLC News webpage.

Measuring inter-beat intervals from ECG signals can provide early warnings for cardiovascular diseases. However, identifying IBIs from noisy signals is difficult, especially when they are heavily distorted by motion noise, which is common in individuals who are highly active. Researchers working on remote health monitoring and wearable devices have identified ECG-ICG fusion signals with high signal-to-noise ratios as the most effective option for IBI estimation. However, creating specialized hardware for ECG-ICG fusion is resource-intensive and may not be feasible for all devices. Previous software-based solutions have attempted to filter out noise from ECG signals have produced subpar results in terms of accuracy when compared to fusion-based approaches. Our team aimed to develop a novel method for ECG signal denoising and IBI estimation, which involves utilizing the Tiramisu model in deep neural networks to achieve enhanced accuracy and reduced error. The Tiramisu model's unique architecture allows it to efficiently process ECG signals and remove noise while preserving vital features associated with IBIs. By using ECG-ICG fusion as a ground truth and comparing our method with leading noise filtering techniques, we demonstrate that our Tiramisu-based approach estimates IBIs with superior accuracy and minimal error, outperforming existing methods even when the ECG signals are undistorted.

To utilize tensors in machine learning, the tensor singular value decomposition (tSVD) must be employed, enabling reductions in dimensionality through techniques like random projections. Currently available randomized methods for calculating the tSVD typically require the same number of passes over the tensor data, regardless of its size. These methods have a memory limitation, restricting their applicability to medium-scale tensor datasets. A new randomized approach to tSVD is presented, utilizing an adaptable number of passes to accommodate diverse tensor sizes. This approach reconstructs the tensor using a low-rank decomposition, where each rank can be estimated using a variable number of samples. Combining these estimates with additional samples ensures an accurate low-rank and pseudo-inverse solution for tSVD. The proposed method's efficiency was validated in testing, demonstrating a favorable balance between memory usage and the number of passes required to achieve a specified relative error in approximation. Furthermore, the calculated tensor singular values and singular tensor values from this method converge rapidly to their actual values, even as computational resources increase. The performance of the method was exemplified in a document classification application using tensor data, resulting in substantial classifying efficiency improvements.

Real-world networks often display dynamic characteristics, which may be brought on by various natural events, such as adding new vertices to social groups or new edges forming between vertices. Traditional network representation techniques typically focus on static networks, but they fall short when applied to changing graphs. To effectively analyze and learn evolving networks, a technique known as embedding evolving graphs is employed, which aims to map vertices into a low-dimensional space for enhanced analysis and learning. This paper thoroughly explores the concept of embedding evolving graphs, specifically devoting attention to the strategies used to capture various changes in such networks. It is shown that effectively handling growing and shrinking networks requires distinct approaches even when the vertices present remain unchanged. Moreover, preserving edge attributes in decreasing edge count scenarios and dealing with loss due to edge removal are also discussed. Finally, a comprehensive summary and future research outlook are provided.

To determine the 7H ground state, we employed the no-core shell model with the A24v6 and JU99/6 and JU06/6 and DaeJ (with relativistic corrections) basis energies. We then calculated the 7H ground state as a 4-charge root in the space of A24 nuclear wave functions using the JU06/6 and DaeJ techniques, with the JU06/6 and DaeJ methods producing identical results. We discovered that the 7H ground state is composed of a single excited 3H to 4n transition, with the 7H ground state energy obtained using the JU06/6 and DaeJ being -7.306 and -7.340 MeV respectively on a phi potential, with both methods providing identical ground state energy. We also obtained a 7H binding energy of -7.5 MeV when using the JU06/6 and DaeJ, with both methods being in agreement. We then calculated a proton decay width of 7H to 3H+4n at 2.6 MeV using the JU06/6 and DaeJ, with both methods agreeing.

The Nirenberg problem on the half sphere S^2S and S^2x S^1, each with a two sphere as its boundary, is being investigated. For the two sphere boundary, a unique blow up solution occurs at infinity. In contrast, when the boundary is the loop S^1, distinct blow up solutions arise at infinity. These solutions differ only in their p and q vector fields directions. Additionally, not all possible p and q directions will yield a blow up solution, a key finding in this investigation.

Deep neural networks are increasingly employed to learn specialized feature representations for a variety of tasks. Research has shown that a good feature representation can significantly improve the performance of downstream tasks. Current deep representations are typically learned with a focus on reducing the distance between actual output and predicted output. This often results in a representation that minimizes the distance between those outputs. This paper presents a novel method for learning deep representations by using the Sinkhorn divergence to balance the needs of multiple tasks. This involves incorporating the Sinkhorn divergence into the loss function of a neural network. This addition provides means to control the level of classifying data and to prevent the over-specialization of models in multi-task environments. Results show that incorporating the Sinkhorn divergence adds benefits in terms of learning general feature representations and improving the performance of downstream tasks. This method was tested in a variety of scenarios, including learning feature representations from pre-trained neural networks that can accurately classify hand-written letters regardless of the language and norm.

To contain the COVID-19 outbreak, England's contact tracing program was introduced in the spring of 2020. The effort involved identifying individuals who had come into close contact with those infected and helped to track the disease's spread by advising these contacts to self-isolate and test positive. The program's success relied heavily on the collaboration between local public health officials, general practitioners, and other healthcare professionals. Three different approaches to engaging these partners were employed across the country, with the northern region focusing on building relationships through in-person meetings, the Midlands and the Isle of Wight relying on email communication, and the rest of England using a combination of both strategies. 

Our research focuses on the contact tracing efforts in the last week of the program, examining the impact of local partnerships on test positivity rates, the total number of tests conducted, and the overall efficiency of the contact tracing efforts. The analysis revealed that the in-person relationship building approach in the northern region and the hybrid model in other areas of England yielded better results compared to the email communication used in the Midlands and the Isle of Wight. Specifically, these areas experienced lower test positivity rates, increased test volumes, and improved contact tracing efficiency. The reasons behind these disparities could be multifaceted, involving factors such as the severity of local outbreaks, availability of resources, constraints posed by government policies, and challenges associated with working in the healthcare sector during the pandemic.

A comprehensive analysis of the Melotte 72 open cluster has been conducted, leveraging precise DR2 velocity data and photometric measurements from the Gaia mission. These new details enhance our understanding of this celestial structure, allowing a detailed examination of spectral types and radial velocities within a 30 parsec radius of the cluster's center. Melotte 72's composition was also expanded upon by incorporating 21 additional stars, bringing the total number of analyzed stars to 66. This analysis sheds light on the nature of seven potential members, revealing that five are probable non-cluster stars while two may be part of Melotte 72. To calculate Melotte 72's age and confirm its chemical properties, we analyzed evolutionary models and elemental composition models, discovering that it is likely younger than previously thought with an estimated age ranging between 1-2 billion years, has a unique metal content with a high proportion of metal, and contains no binary stars within its innermost region. Moreover, we determined that Melotte 72's turn-off and subgiant sequences are defined by specific hue and brightness values. Melotte 72's horizontal-branch sequence was also identified but it's not prominent. The three dimensional spatial arrangement of the Melotte 72's member stars and other properties were further investigated to calculate the physical characteristics of the Melotte 72's star cluster.
